A1.title: Classifying Rational & Irrational Numbers | Real Number System | Algebra 1 Notes
A1.ican: classify a real number as natural, whole, integer, rational, and/or irrational.
A1.key_rule: Simplify first. Then find the narrowest set that holds the number, and name every set that contains it.
A1.key_rule_hint: Every real number is rational or irrational, never both.

watch.text: Classify √25.
watch.wrong: √25 has a root sign: irrational, real
watch.wrong_why: A root sign alone does not decide it.
watch.right_why: 5 × 5 = 25. The square root of a whole number is irrational unless the number is a perfect square.

A1.learn: Students learn to simplify a number first, then name every set it belongs to: natural, whole, integer, rational or irrational, and real.
A1.watchout: a wrong and a right classification of √25 side by side; the wrong one calls it irrational because of its root sign, but √25 = 5 is natural, whole, integer, rational and real.
mistakes: Calls a number irrational just because it has a root sign
Treats any number with no fraction part, negatives included, as whole
Calls every never-ending decimal irrational, even ones that repeat
Counts 0 as a natural number
Treats a decimal close to π, such as 3.14, as π itself

standards.text: Explain why the sum or product of two rational numbers is rational; that the sum of a rational number and an irrational number is irrational; and that the product of a nonzero rational number and an irrational number is irrational.

A2.skill: Sums and Products of Rational and Irrational Numbers
A2.title: Sums & Products of Rational & Irrational Numbers | Closure Property | Algebra 1
A2.ican: explain and apply the closure rules for sums and products of rational and irrational numbers.
A2.key_rule: Rational + rational and rational × rational are rational: the rationals are closed. Rational + irrational is irrational, and so is a nonzero rational × irrational.
A2.key_rule_hint: Two irrationals follow no rule (√2 × √2 = 2, but √2 + √3 is irrational): test each one.

watch.text: Is 0 × √7 rational or irrational?
watch.wrong_why: The rule needs a nonzero rational.
watch.right_why: Zero times any number is 0.

A2.learn: Students learn to decide whether a sum or a product is rational or irrational: they name its case, test a product for a zero factor, and work out any pair of irrationals.
A2.watchout: a wrong and a right answer to whether 0 × √7 is rational side by side; the wrong one calls it irrational, but 0 × √7 = 0, which is rational.
mistakes: Lets an irrational factor decide a product without checking for a zero factor
Makes up a rule for two irrationals instead of working them out
Calls a repeating decimal irrational because it never ends
Calls a nonzero rational times an irrational rational
Classifies a rounded decimal instead of the exact number

standards.text: Explain why the sum or product of two rational numbers is rational; that the sum of a rational number and an irrational number is irrational; and that the product of a nonzero rational number and an irrational number is irrational.

A3.title: Evaluating Algebraic Expressions Worksheet | Algebra 1 Notes, Slides & Key
A3.ican: substitute given values into an algebraic expression and simplify with order of operations.
A3.key_rule: Put each value in parentheses where its letter was. Then simplify in order: inside ( ) first, then exponents, then × and ÷, then + and −, each left to right.
A3.key_rule_hint: A negative value squared is positive: (−3)² = 9, but −3² = −9.

watch.text: Evaluate x² when x = −6.
watch.wrong_why: Only the 6 was squared; the − stayed outside.
watch.right_why: Keep the value's sign inside the ( ).

A3.learn: Students learn to evaluate an expression or formula for given values, negatives included, by putting each value in parentheses and simplifying in order.
A3.watchout: a wrong and a right evaluation of x² when x = −6 side by side; the wrong one writes −6² = −36, squaring only the 6 instead of (−6)² = 36.
mistakes: Squares a negative value without putting it in parentheses
Loses the sign when subtracting a negative
Squares the negative sign in −x²
Treats an even power of a negative number as negative
Ignores the parentheses in a formula and works out of order

standards.text: Interpret parts of an expression, such as terms, factors, and coefficients.

A4.title: Properties of Real Numbers & Operations | Distributive Property | Algebra 1
A4.ican: name the property that justifies a step and apply the Distributive Property correctly.
A4.key_rule: Name the property by what changed from one side to the other. To distribute, multiply the number in front by every term inside the ( ).
A4.key_rule_hint: Commutative swaps two numbers. Associative keeps the order and moves the parentheses.

watch.text: Distribute 3(x + 4).
watch.wrong_why: The 3 multiplied only the x.
watch.right_why: The 3 multiplies every term: 3 × 4 = 12.

A4.learn: Students learn to name the property behind each step and distribute a number to every term inside the parentheses.
A4.watchout: a wrong and a right distribution of 3(x + 4) side by side; the wrong one writes 3x + 4, multiplying only the x instead of both terms.
mistakes: Multiplies only the first term inside the parentheses
Calls a regrouping commutative when only the parentheses moved
Mixes up the identity and inverse properties
Loses a sign when distributing a negative number
Calls any equation with parentheses the Distributive Property

standards.text: Explain each step in solving a simple equation as following from the equality of numbers asserted at the previous step, starting from the assumption that the original equation has a solution. Construct a viable argument to justify a solution method.

A5.skill: Combining Like Terms and the Distributive Property
A5.title: Combining Like Terms & Distributive Property | Simplifying Expressions Algebra 1
A5.ican: distribute, then combine like terms to fully simplify an expression.
A5.key_rule: First distribute: the factor in front multiplies each term inside the ( ). Then combine like terms: add their coefficients and keep the variable part.
A5.key_rule_hint: A constant never joins an x term: 6x + 10 is already simplified.

watch.text: Simplify 3(x + 4) + 2x.
watch.wrong_why: The 12 has no x, but it was added to the x coefficients.
watch.right_why: Only 3x and 2x are like terms. The 12 stays.

A5.learn: Students learn to simplify an expression all the way: they distribute to each term inside the parentheses, then combine like terms, keeping x² terms, x terms and constants apart.
A5.watchout: a wrong and a right simplification of 3(x + 4) + 2x side by side; the wrong one adds the constant 12 to the x terms and gets 17x instead of 5x + 12.
mistakes: Joins a constant to the x terms
Combines x² terms with x terms
Loses a sign when the factor in front is negative
Multiplies only the first term inside the parentheses
Reads x times x as 2x instead of x²

standards.text: Interpret parts of an expression, such as terms, factors, and coefficients.

A6.title: Translating Algebraic Expressions Worksheet | Writing Expressions | Algebra 1
A6.ican: translate a verbal phrase into an algebraic expression, watching for phrases that reverse the order.
A6.key_rule: Keep the order you read, except after less than, fewer than and subtracted from: they reverse it. A sum or difference multiplied, divided or squared as a whole goes in parentheses.
A6.key_rule_hint: Test it: 8 less than 20 is 12, which is 20 − 8, not 8 − 20.

watch.text: Write an expression for “5 less than a number x.”
watch.wrong_why: The words were written in the order they were read.
watch.right_why: Less than reverses the order: start with x, then take 5 away.

A6.learn: Students learn to write an expression from words: they keep the order they read, reverse it after less than, fewer than and subtracted from, and put a whole sum or difference in parentheses.
A6.watchout: a wrong and a right expression for 5 less than a number x side by side; the wrong one writes 5 − x in reading order instead of x − 5.
mistakes: Writes less than, fewer than or subtracted from in reading order
Leaves out the parentheses around a sum that is multiplied
Squares only the letter instead of the whole difference
Takes a monthly discount off once instead of every month
Halves only the last number instead of the whole amount

standards.text: Interpret parts of an expression, such as terms, factors, and coefficients.

A7.title: Parts of an Algebraic Expression Worksheet | Interpreting Expressions Algebra 1
A7.ican: name the terms, factors, coefficients and constant term of an expression, and say what they mean.
A7.key_rule: A term ends where a + or − sign outside ( ) begins. The parts multiplied inside one term are its factors, not separate terms.

watch.text: How many terms does 7ab have?
watch.wrong_why: 7, a and b are multiplied, so they are factors.
watch.right_why: No + or − splits it, so it stays one term.

A7.learn: Students learn to tell terms from factors, give each coefficient with its sign, and say what a coefficient and a constant mean in a real situation.
A7.watchout: a wrong and a right count of the terms in 7ab side by side; the wrong one counts 3 terms, but 7, a and b are factors of 1 term.
mistakes: Counts factors as separate terms
Drops the sign of a coefficient
Splits a term at a sign inside parentheses
Swaps the meanings of the coefficient and the constant in a context
Leaves the sign off a constant term

standards.text: Interpret complicated expressions by viewing one or more of their parts as a single entity. For example, interpret P(1+r)ⁿ as the product of P and a factor not depending on P.

A8.title: Dimensional Analysis Worksheet | Unit Conversions & Precision | Algebra 1 Notes
A8.ican: convert units with conversion factors that cancel, and report an answer only as precisely as its measurements allow.
A8.key_rule: In each factor, put the unit you need to cancel on the opposite side (top or bottom) from where it is now. The units left at the end are the units you want.
A8.key_rule_hint: Report an answer no more precisely than its measurements.

watch.text: Convert 4 ft to inches.
watch.wrong_why: Nothing cancels: ft is on top twice.
watch.right_why: ft in the denominator cancels the ft you have.

A8.learn: Students learn to convert units and rates with a chain of factors that cancel the unit they have, choose a sensible unit, and give a result no more precisely than its measurement.
A8.watchout: a wrong and a right conversion of 4 ft to inches side by side; the wrong one multiplies by 1 ft / 12 in, so nothing cancels, instead of 12 in / 1 ft.
mistakes: Uses a conversion factor upside down
Treats a converted measurement as more precise than the original
Changes only one unit of a rate
Stops after one factor in a multi-step conversion chain
Writes digits the measurement does not have

standards.text: Use units as a way to understand problems and to guide the solution of multi-step problems; choose and interpret units consistently in formulas; choose and interpret the scale and the origin in graphs and data displays.
Define appropriate quantities for the purpose of descriptive modeling.
Choose a level of accuracy appropriate to limitations on measurement when reporting quantities.

A9.title: Solving One-Step Equations with Integers & Decimals Worksheet | Algebra 1 Notes
A9.ican: solve a one-step equation by doing the inverse operation to both sides.
A9.key_rule: Find the operation done to the variable. Undo it with its inverse, done to both sides.
A9.key_rule_hint: Add or subtract the same number on both sides, or multiply or divide both sides by the same nonzero number.

watch.text: Solve x − 7 = 5.
watch.wrong_why: 7 was added to the left side only, so the scale tips.
watch.right_why: Add 7 to both sides. Check: 12 − 7 = 5.

A9.learn: Students learn to solve one-step equations with negative numbers, decimals and the variable on either side, by undoing the operation on both sides, then checking the solution.
A9.watchout: a wrong and a right solution of x − 7 = 5 side by side; the wrong one adds 7 to the left side only and gets x = 5 instead of x = 12.
mistakes: Changes one side of the equation only
Repeats the operation instead of undoing it
Gets the sign of a quotient wrong
Reads −x = 13 as x = 13
Divides when the variable is divided instead of multiplying

standards.text: Solve linear equations and inequalities in one variable, including equations with coefficients represented by letters.

A10.title: Solving Two-Step Equations with Integers Worksheet | Algebra 1 Notes & Key
A10.ican: solve a two-step equation by undoing the operations in reverse order.
A10.key_rule: To solve ax + b = c, undo in reverse order: first the adding or subtracting, then the multiplying. Do each move to both sides.
A10.key_rule_hint: For x/a + b = c, the second move is to multiply both sides by a.

watch.text: Solve 5x + 15 = 40.
watch.wrong_why: The 5x and the 40 were divided by 5, but the 15 was not.
watch.right_why: Subtract 15 first, then divide by 5. Check: 5(5) + 15 = 40.

A10.learn: Students learn to solve two-step equations, including negative coefficients and the variable on either side, by undoing the operations in reverse order, then checking the solution.
A10.watchout: a wrong and a right solution of 5x + 15 = 40 side by side; the wrong one divides 5x and 40 by 5 but not the 15, and gets x = −7.
mistakes: Divides only some of the terms by the coefficient
Undoes an operation with the same operation
Gets the sign of a quotient wrong
Divides when the variable is divided instead of multiplying
Drops the minus sign in front of the x term

standards.text: Solve linear equations and inequalities in one variable, including equations with coefficients represented by letters.

A11.title: Solving Multi-Step Linear Equations with Distributive Property | Algebra 1 Notes
A11.ican: simplify each side by distributing and combining like terms, then solve the equation.
A11.key_rule: First simplify each side: distribute, then combine like terms. Then undo in reverse order: the adding or subtracting first.
A11.key_rule_hint: A negative in front multiplies every term inside, sign and all: −2(x − 5) = −2x + 10.

watch.text: Solve 2(x + 9) + x = 30.
watch.wrong_why: The 2 multiplied the x but not the 9.
watch.right_why: The 2 multiplies both terms in the ( ). Then 3x = 12.

A11.learn: Students learn to solve multi-step equations: they distribute and combine like terms to simplify a side first, then undo the operations in reverse order and verify the solution.
A11.watchout: a wrong and a right solution of 2(x + 9) + x = 30 side by side; the wrong one multiplies the x by 2 but not the 9, and gets x = 7.
mistakes: Multiplies only the first term inside the parentheses
Loses the sign when the number in front of parentheses is negative
Changes only the first sign after a minus in front of parentheses
Drops the sign of a negative term when combining like terms
Multiplies only the number term inside the parentheses

standards.text: Solve linear equations and inequalities in one variable, including equations with coefficients represented by letters.

A12.skill: Equations with Variables on Both Sides
A12.title: Solving Equations with Variables on Both Sides Worksheet | Algebra 1 Notes & Key
A12.ican: solve an equation with variables on both sides by collecting the x terms on one side.
A12.key_rule: Remove the x term from one side by doing the same to both sides. Then solve what is left in reverse order.
A12.key_rule_hint: Every equation here has different x coefficients on its two sides, so an x term is always left.

watch.text: Solve 6x + 4 = 2x + 24.
watch.wrong_why: The 2x was taken off the right but added to the left.
watch.right_why: Subtract 2x from both sides. Then 4x = 20.

A12.learn: Students learn to solve equations with x terms on both sides: they remove an x term from one side by doing the same to both sides, then solve what is left and test it in both sides.
A12.watchout: a wrong and a right solution of 6x + 4 = 2x + 24 side by side; the wrong one takes 2x off the right but adds it to the left, getting 8x.
mistakes: Joins x terms across the equal sign
Undoes a subtraction by subtracting again
Adds a lone variable to the other x term instead of subtracting it
Drops a term when simplifying one side
Checks the solution in only one side

standards.text: Solve linear equations and inequalities in one variable, including equations with coefficients represented by letters.

A13.title: Solving Equations with Fractions and Decimals Worksheet | Algebra 1 Notes & Key
A13.ican: clear the fractions or decimals from an equation, then solve it.
A13.key_rule: Multiply every term on both sides by the LCD, or by a power of ten for decimals. Then solve.
A13.key_rule_hint: The whole numbers are terms too: in x/5 + 1 = 3, the 1 and the 3 are multiplied by 5.

watch.text: Solve x/2 + x/4 = 6.
watch.wrong_why: The 4 multiplied the fractions but not the 6.
watch.right_why: Multiply every term by 4, the 6 too. Then 3x = 24.

A13.learn: Students learn to clear the fractions or decimals from an equation by multiplying every term on both sides by the LCD or a power of ten, then solve it and verify it in the original equation.
A13.watchout: a wrong and a right solution of x/2 + x/4 = 6 side by side; the wrong one multiplies the fractions by 4 but not the 6, and gets x = 2.
mistakes: Multiplies the fractions by the LCD but not the whole numbers
Multiplies only the decimal with the variable by a power of ten
Skips a whole-number term when the variable is on both sides
Checks the answer in the cleared equation only

standards.text: Solve linear equations and inequalities in one variable, including equations with coefficients represented by letters.

A14.skill: No Solution and Infinitely Many Solutions
A14.title: Number of Solutions | One Solution, No Solution, Infinite Solutions | Algebra 1
A14.ican: tell whether an equation has one solution, no solution, or infinitely many solutions.
A14.key_rule: If the x terms drop out, the answer is not a value of x. A false statement left means no solution; a true one means all real numbers.
A14.key_rule_hint: Reaching 0 = 0 does not mean x = 0: it is true for every x.

watch.wrong_why: 0 = 0 has no x in it. It does not say what x is.
watch.right_why: Both sides are the same, so every x works. Try x = 1: 12 and 12.

A14.learn: Students learn to solve an equation and read its ending: x = a number (one solution), a false statement (no solution), or a true statement (all real numbers, infinitely many solutions).
A14.watchout: a wrong and a right solution of 2(x + 5) = 2x + 10 side by side; the wrong one reads 0 = 0 as x = 0 instead of all real numbers.
mistakes: Reads 0 = 0 as x = 0
Mixes up the no-solution and all-real-numbers endings
Joins x terms across the equal sign
Undoes a subtraction by subtracting again
Picks a missing value that matches the x terms but not the constants

standards.text: Solve linear equations and inequalities in one variable, including equations with coefficients represented by letters.

A15.skill: Justifying Each Step in a Solution
A15.title: Algebraic Proofs Worksheet | Properties of Equality | Justifying Steps Algebra 1
A15.ican: name the property that justifies each step when I solve an equation.
A15.key_rule: A reason names the property that makes a step legal, never the numbers in it. The first line's reason is Given.
A15.key_rule_hint: Its reason: Addition Property of Equality, not add 4.

watch.text: Give the reason for going from 3x + 7 = 22 to 3x = 15.
watch.wrong_why: That names the operation, not the property.
watch.right_why: Both sides had 7 subtracted, and this property says they stay equal.

A15.learn: Students learn to give a reason for every step of a solution: a Property of Equality for a move made on both sides, the Distributive Property or Combine Like Terms for a side rewritten, and the Symmetric Property for switched sides.
A15.watchout: a wrong and a right reason for going from 3x + 7 = 22 to 3x = 15; the wrong one names the operation, subtract 7, not the Subtraction Property of Equality.
mistakes: Writes the operation instead of the property as the reason
Calls a both-sides step the Distributive Property
Joins x terms across the equal sign
Multiplies only the first term inside the parentheses
Undoes a subtraction by subtracting again

standards.text: Explain each step in solving a simple equation as following from the equality of numbers asserted at the previous step, starting from the assumption that the original equation has a solution. Construct a viable argument to justify a solution method.

A16.title: Literal Equations Worksheet | Solving for a Variable | Algebra 1 Notes & Key
A16.ican: solve a formula for any one of its letters, using the same moves as solving for x.
A16.key_rule: Treat the other letters as numbers. Undo what is added or subtracted first, then divide the whole side by what multiplies the letter.

watch.text: Solve 4x + 2y = 10 for y.
watch.wrong_why: Only the 10 was divided by 2. The 4x was not.
watch.right_why: Divide the whole side by 2: both terms.

A16.learn: Students learn to rearrange a formula to solve for a chosen letter: they treat the other letters as numbers, undo what is added or subtracted, then divide the whole side, and say when a letter cannot be 0.
A16.watchout: a wrong and a right solution of 4x + 2y = 10 for y; the wrong one divides only the 10 by 2 and gets y = 5 − 4x instead of 5 − 2x.
mistakes: Divides or multiplies only part of a side, leaving a term out
Divides by 2 to undo a multiplication by 1/2
Adds a term instead of subtracting it from both sides
Divides by a letter without saying it cannot be 0

standards.text: Rearrange formulas to highlight a quantity of interest, using the same reasoning as in solving equations. For example, rearrange Ohm's law V = IR to highlight resistance R.

A17.title: Writing and Solving Linear Equations from Word Problems Worksheet | Algebra 1
A17.ican: turn a word problem into an equation, solve it and check the answer in the story.
A17.key_rule: Name the unknown and its units. Write one equation for the whole situation, solve it, then check the answer in the story, not only in the equation.
A17.key_rule_hint: A fee paid one time is added once; a price paid each month multiplies m.

watch.text: Ana has 3 times Ben's cards. Together they have 48. How many has Ben?
watch.wrong_why: 3b is only Ana's cards. Together means Ben's plus Ana's.
watch.right_why: Check in the story: 12 + 36 = 48 cards.

A17.learn: Students learn to define a variable with its units, write one equation that says everything the story says, solve it and verify the answer in the story's words.
A17.watchout: a wrong and a right equation for Ana having 3 times Ben's cards with 48 cards together, side by side; the wrong one writes 3b = 48, counting only Ana's cards.
mistakes: Writes an equation for only part of the story
Swaps the one-time fee and the amount for each item
Answers a different quantity from the one the question asks for
Checks the answer only in the equation, not in the story

standards.text: Create equations and inequalities in one variable and use them to solve problems. Include equations arising from linear and quadratic functions, and simple rational and exponential functions.

A18.title: Solving Absolute Value Equations Worksheet | Algebra 1 Notes, Slides & Key
A18.ican: solve absolute value equations, including when there are two solutions, one or none.
A18.key_rule: Get the absolute value alone. Then read c: if c > 0, solve two equations, the inside = c and the inside = −c; if c = 0, solve one; if c < 0, there is no solution.
A18.key_rule_hint: Check each answer in the first equation: both must make it true.

watch.text: Solve |x + 4| = 9.
watch.wrong_why: That is one equation. The inside can also be −9.
watch.right_why: Both check: |5 + 4| = 9 and |−13 + 4| = 9.

A18.learn: Students learn to solve |ax + b| = c: they get the absolute value alone first, then solve two equations when c is positive, one when c is 0, and none when c is negative, and verify every answer.
A18.watchout: a wrong and a right solution of |x + 4| = 9 side by side; the wrong one solves only x + 4 = 9 and misses x = −13.
mistakes: Solves only one of the two equations
Splits into two equations before the absolute value is alone
Takes the opposite of the first answer as the second answer
Splits into two equations when the absolute value equals a negative
Gives two answers when the absolute value equals 0

standards.text: Solve linear equations and inequalities in one variable, including equations with coefficients represented by letters.

A19.title: Solving and Graphing Inequalities Worksheet | One & Two-Step | Algebra 1 Notes
A19.ican: solve one- and two-step inequalities and graph the solution set.
A19.key_rule: Solve with an equation's moves, multiplying or dividing only by positive numbers here. The answer is a set: write x ≤ 2, not x = 2, then graph it and test a number from the ray.
A19.key_rule_hint: ≤ and ≥ include the boundary; < and > leave it out.

watch.text: Solve x + 8 > 15.
watch.wrong_why: x = 7 is only the boundary, and 7 is not even a solution.
watch.right_why: Every number above 7 works: 8 + 8 = 16, and 16 > 15.

A19.learn: Students learn to solve one- and two-step inequalities with an equation's moves, write the answer as a set such as x ≤ 2, graph it with the right circle and ray, and test a number from the ray.
A19.watchout: a wrong and a right solution of x + 8 > 15 side by side; the wrong one gives only the boundary, x = 7, instead of the solution set x > 7.
mistakes: Writes the boundary as the answer instead of a solution set
Reverses the symbol after adding or subtracting a negative number
Uses a closed circle where the boundary is not a solution
Rounds the wrong way when a story needs a whole number
Undoes a step with the wrong operation

standards.text: Solve linear equations and inequalities in one variable, including equations with coefficients represented by letters.

A20.skill: Multi-Step Inequalities and the Reversal Rule
A20.title: Solving Multi-Step Linear Inequalities Worksheet | Algebra 1 Notes & Answer Key
A20.ican: solve multi-step inequalities and reverse the symbol only when I multiply or divide by a negative.
A20.key_rule: Solve as you would an equation. When you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number, reverse the symbol; adding or subtracting never reverses it.
A20.key_rule_hint: Test a number from your answer in the first inequality: a missed reversal fails at once.

watch.text: Solve 6x − 1 < −19.
watch.wrong_why: It reverses the symbol, but 6 is positive.
watch.right_why: Divide by positive 6: the symbol stays. Test −4: −25 < −19.

A20.learn: Students learn to solve multi-step inequalities, reverse the symbol only when they multiply or divide both sides by a negative number, and test a number from their answer.
A20.watchout: a wrong and a right solution of 6x − 1 < −19 side by side; the wrong one reverses the symbol even though 6 is positive.
mistakes: Divides by a negative and keeps the inequality symbol
Reverses the symbol just because a number is negative
Gets a sign wrong when distributing a negative
Gives an excluded boundary as the greatest integer solution

standards.text: Solve linear equations and inequalities in one variable, including equations with coefficients represented by letters.

A21.title: Compound Inequalities Worksheet | Solving & Graphing And/Or | Algebra 1 Notes
A21.ican: solve compound inequalities and graph AND and OR solution sets.
A21.key_rule: Solve each part. AND keeps the numbers that make both parts true; OR keeps the numbers that make either part true. In a chain, do every step to all three parts.
A21.key_rule_hint: Divide a chain by a negative and reverse each symbol: −2 < −x < 3 becomes 2 > x > −3.

watch.text: Describe the solution set of 5 < x < 2.
watch.wrong_why: It reads the chain as a range, but the bigger number is on the left.
watch.right: x > 5 and x < 2: no number does both, so no solution
watch.right_why: Test 3: 5 < 3 is false. Every number fails one of the two parts.

A21.learn: Students learn to solve a compound inequality, keep the overlap for AND and every number either part allows for OR, graph it as one piece or two rays, and test a number.
A21.watchout: a wrong and a right reading of 5 < x < 2; the wrong one calls it the numbers between 2 and 5, but no number is both above 5 and below 2.
mistakes: Reads a chain as a range when its bigger number is on the left
Turns an OR inequality into a between
Does a step to the middle part of a chain only
Divides a chain by a negative without reversing both symbols

standards.text: Solve linear equations and inequalities in one variable, including equations with coefficients represented by letters.

A22.title: Solving Absolute Value Inequalities Worksheet | Graphing | Algebra 1 Notes & Key
A22.ican: solve absolute value inequalities and graph the one-piece or two-piece answer.
A22.key_rule: Get the absolute value alone. For b > 0, less than: the inside is between −b and b, one piece; greater than: the inside is less than −b or greater than b, two rays.
A22.key_rule_hint: If b is negative, read the symbol: < has no solution, > is all real numbers.

watch.text: Solve |x − 2| > 6.
watch.wrong_why: One piece is the answer to < 6, not to > 6.
watch.right: x − 2 < −6 or x − 2 > 6, so x < −4 or x > 8
watch.right_why: More than 6 from 2 is two rays. Test 9: |9 − 2| = 7, and 7 > 6.

A22.learn: Students learn to get the absolute value alone, read less than as within (one piece) and greater than as beyond (two rays), read a negative right side exactly, and test a number.
A22.watchout: a wrong and a right solution of |x − 2| > 6 side by side; the wrong one writes one piece, −4 < x < 8, which answers less than 6, not greater than 6.
mistakes: Solves a greater-than inequality as one piece, like a less-than
Reads the center with the wrong sign
Misreads an absolute value compared with a negative number
Leaves the symbol unreversed on the negative side

standards.text: Solve linear equations and inequalities in one variable, including equations with coefficients represented by letters.

A23.skill: Writing Inequalities and Constraints from Context
A23.title: Inequality Word Problems | Writing Inequalities from Context | Algebra 1 Notes
A23.ican: turn a situation into an inequality and say which answers it actually allows.
A23.key_rule: Name the variable and its units. Let each phrase set the symbol, solve, then keep only the values the situation allows.
A23.key_rule_hint: When the story counts things, test whole numbers in it: under a cap, keep the greatest that fits; to reach a minimum, the least that does.

watch.text: A lift carries at most 8 people. Write an inequality for the number of people, p.
watch.wrong_why: < leaves 8 out, but 8 people may ride.
watch.right_why: At most 8 means 8 or fewer: 8 itself counts.

A23.learn: Students learn to name a variable with its units, let each phrase choose the symbol, solve, and keep only the answers the situation allows, checking a whole number in the story.
A23.watchout: a wrong and a right inequality for a lift that carries at most 8 people side by side; the wrong one writes p < 8, which leaves out 8 people.
mistakes: Uses < for at most instead of ≤
Uses ≥ for more than instead of >
Leaves out a one-time fee
Rounds the wrong way or keeps part of an object a story counts whole

standards.text: Create equations and inequalities in one variable and use them to solve problems. Include equations arising from linear and quadratic functions, and simple rational and exponential functions.

Represent constraints by equations or inequalities, and by systems of equations and/or inequalities, and interpret solutions as viable or nonviable options in a modeling context. For example, represent inequalities describing nutritional and cost constraints on combinations of different foods.

A24.skill: Graphing Linear Inequalities in Two Variables
A24.title: Graphing Linear Inequalities in Two Variables Worksheet | Algebra 1 Notes & Key
A24.ican: graph a linear inequality in two variables and shade the correct side of the boundary.
A24.key_rule: Graph the boundary: solid for ≤ or ≥, dashed for < or >. Test a point off the line: if it is true, shade its side; if it is false, shade the other side.
A24.key_rule_hint: (0, 0) is the easiest point to test, unless the line passes through it.

watch.text: Graph 2x − y > 4. Which side is shaded?
watch.wrong_why: That rule only works once y is alone.
watch.right_why: Dividing by −1 reverses it. Test (0, 0): 0 > 4 is false.

A24.learn: Students learn to graph the boundary line of a two-variable inequality, solid or dashed, and shade the side a test point shows is true, getting y alone first.
A24.watchout: a wrong and a right graph of 2x − y > 4 side by side; the wrong one shades above because of the >, but solving gives y < 2x − 4, so shade below.
mistakes: Shades by the symbol before y is alone
Keeps the symbol after dividing by a negative
Mixes up solid and dashed boundary lines
Counts a point on a dashed line as a solution
Uses a test point that lies on the boundary line

standards.text: Graph the solutions to a linear inequality in two variables as a half-plane (excluding the boundary in the case of a strict inequality), and graph the solution set to a system of linear inequalities in two variables as the intersection of the corresponding half-planes.

A25.title: Graphing Systems of Linear Inequalities Worksheet | Algebra 1 Notes & Answer Key
A25.ican: graph a system of linear inequalities and find the region where both are true.
A25.key_rule: Graph each inequality on one grid. The solutions are the overlap: the points that make both true.
A25.key_rule_hint: One false test is enough: a point in only one shaded region is not a solution.

watch.text: Is (4, 1) a solution of y ≤ x + 2 and x + y < 4?
watch.wrong_why: It was checked in only one inequality.
watch.right: x + y < 4: 4 + 1 < 4 is false, so no
watch.right_why: A solution must make both true; (4, 1) fails x + y < 4.

A25.learn: Students learn to graph two inequalities on one grid, find the overlap where both are true, and test a point in both inequalities.
A25.watchout: a wrong and a right test of whether (4, 1) solves y ≤ x + 2 and x + y < 4; the wrong one tests only the first inequality and says yes.
mistakes: Checks a point in only one inequality
Reads a solid boundary as dashed, or a dashed one as solid
Counts a point on a dashed boundary as a solution
Shades every region either inequality covers instead of the overlap

standards.text: Graph the solutions to a linear inequality in two variables as a half-plane (excluding the boundary in the case of a strict inequality), and graph the solution set to a system of linear inequalities in two variables as the intersection of the corresponding half-planes.

A26.title: Domain and Range Worksheet | Relations and Functions | Algebra 1 Notes & Key
A26.ican: name the domain and range of a relation and decide whether it is a function.
A26.key_rule: Write each set in braces, each value once, smallest first. A relation is a function when no input has two different outputs.
A26.key_rule_hint: A y-value may repeat: (1, 5) and (2, 5) can both be in a function.

watch.wrong_why: The test never looks at repeated outputs.
watch.right: each input has one output: yes, it is a function
watch.right_why: Only one input with two outputs would break it.

A26.learn: Students learn to write the domain and range of a relation as sets and decide whether it is a function by checking each input.
A26.watchout: a wrong and a right answer to whether (1, 6), (2, 6), (3, 6) is a function side by side; the wrong one says no because the output 6 repeats.
mistakes: Rules out a function because an output repeats
Swaps the domain and the range
Lists a repeated value twice in a set
Calls a relation a function when one input has two outputs

standards.text: Understand that a function from one set (called the domain) to another set (called the range) assigns to each element of the domain exactly one element of the range. If f is a function and x is an element of its domain, then f(x) denotes the output of f corresponding to the input x. The graph of f is the graph of the equation y = f(x).

A27.title: Is It a Function or Not? Identifying Functions | Mapping Diagrams | Algebra 1
A27.ican: read a mapping diagram and decide whether the relation is a function.
A27.key_rule: Count the arrows that leave each input. One from every input: a function. Two from any one input: not a function.
A27.key_rule_hint: Arrows landing on the same output never matter.
A27.key_formula: count arrows OUT of each input

watch.text: The inputs 2, 5 and 9 each have one arrow, all landing on 4. Is it a function?
watch.wrong_why: That counts arrows landing, not leaving.
watch.right: one arrow leaves each input: yes, it is a function
watch.right_why: Arrows may land together on one output.

A27.learn: Students learn to read the ordered pairs in a mapping diagram and decide whether it is a function by counting the arrows that leave each input.
A27.watchout: a wrong and a right answer for a mapping diagram where inputs 2, 5 and 9 all point to 4; the wrong one says not a function because three arrows land on 4.
mistakes: Counts the arrows that land on an output instead of those leaving an input
Reads an arrow backwards when writing ordered pairs
Checks only the first input or two
Adds an arrow that is already drawn

standards.text: Understand that a function from one set (called the domain) to another set (called the range) assigns to each element of the domain exactly one element of the range. If f is a function and x is an element of its domain, then f(x) denotes the output of f corresponding to the input x. The graph of f is the graph of the equation y = f(x).

A28.title: Function Notation Worksheet | From a Table and a Graph | Algebra 1 Notes & Key
A28.ican: read and use f(x) notation to find an output from a rule, a table or a graph.
A28.key_rule: In f(3) = 7, the 3 in the parentheses is the input and 7 is the output.
A28.key_rule_hint: f names the function, like a label on a machine. It never multiplies.

watch.text: f(x) = 4x − 1. Find f(5).
watch.wrong_why: f is a name, not a number to multiply.
watch.right_why: 5 is the input: put it in for x.

A28.learn: Students learn to read f(x) as the output for the input x, find values from a rule, a table or a graph, and find the input for a given output.
A28.watchout: a wrong and a right way to find f(5) for f(x) = 4x − 1 side by side; the wrong one writes 5f, treating f as a number, instead of 4(5) − 1 = 19.
mistakes: Reads f(x) as f times x
Writes the input beside the coefficient as digits instead of multiplying
Gives the output when the input is asked for
Adds the numbers in a rule and forgets the input

standards.text: Use function notation, evaluate functions for inputs in their domains, and interpret statements that use function notation in terms of a context.

A29.title: Evaluating Functions Worksheet | Function Notation | Algebra 1 Notes & Key
A29.ican: put an input into a function rule in parentheses, signs and all, and tell evaluating from solving.
A29.key_rule: Write the input in parentheses wherever x is. In f(7) the 7 goes in; in f(x) = 7 the 7 is the output, so solve.
A29.key_rule_hint: Before you start, ask which side of the = the number is on.

watch.text: g(x) = x² + 2. Find g(−5).
watch.wrong_why: −5² squares only the 5.
watch.right_why: (−5)² = 25: the sign is squared too.

A29.learn: Students learn to evaluate a function for any input, writing it in parentheses so its sign goes in too, and tell finding f(a) from finding the x that gives f(x) = k.
A29.watchout: a wrong and a right evaluation of g(−5) for g(x) = x² + 2 side by side; the wrong one writes −5² + 2 = −23 instead of (−5)² + 2 = 27.
mistakes: Squares a negative input without parentheses
Substitutes a number that is the output as the input
Solves for x when the number is the input
Drops a minus sign when two negatives meet

standards.text: Use function notation, evaluate functions for inputs in their domains, and interpret statements that use function notation in terms of a context.

A30.skill: Writing a Function Rule from a Table
A30.title: Writing a Function Rule from a Table Worksheet | Input Output Tables | Algebra 1
A30.ican: write the rule for a table by finding the step and the start, then checking every row.
A30.key_rule: y = (step)x + (start). The step multiplies x; the start is y at x = 0. Then check the rule on every row.
A30.key_rule_hint: If x jumps by 2, the step is the change in y ÷ 2.

watch.text: The pairs are (1, 5), (2, 8) and (3, 11). Write the rule.
watch.wrong: up 3 each time, so y = x + 3
watch.wrong_why: At x = 1 that gives 4, not 5.
watch.right_why: The step multiplies x; every row checks.

A30.learn: Students learn to find a table's step (the change in y for each 1 in x) and its start (y at x = 0), write y = (step)x + (start), and test the rule on every row.
A30.watchout: a wrong and a right rule for the pairs (1, 5), (2, 8), (3, 11); the wrong one adds the step, y = x + 3, instead of y = 3x + 2.
mistakes: Adds the step instead of multiplying x by it
Takes the y change as the step when x jumps by more than 1
Checks only the rows the rule was built from
Uses the first output as the start instead of y at x = 0

standards.text: Write a function that describes a relationship between two quantities.

A31.title: Key Features of Functions & Graphs | Interpreting & Analyzing Graphs | Algebra 1
A31.ican: find the intercepts, the maximum or minimum, and where a graph rises, falls, and is positive or negative.
A31.key_rule: Read left to right; give each interval in x-values, with <. A maximum or minimum is a point; its value is its height.
A31.key_rule_hint: A turn or a crossing is in neither interval, so use < at both ends.
A31.key_formula: max (a, b): value b, at x = a

watch.text: A graph's lowest point is (2, −3). Give the minimum value and where it occurs.
watch.wrong_why: x = 2 is where it occurs, not its value.
watch.right_why: The value is the y-coordinate of (2, −3).

A31.learn: Students learn to read a graph's intercepts and turning point as points, give a maximum or minimum value and where it occurs, and give the intervals where the graph increases, decreases, is positive and is negative.
A31.watchout: a wrong and a right answer for a graph whose lowest point is (2, −3) side by side; the wrong one gives the minimum as x = 2 instead of the value −3.
mistakes: Gives where a maximum or minimum occurs as its value
Reads an interval from right to left
Gives the interval below the x-axis as positive
Mixes up the y-intercept and the x-intercept

standards.text: For a function that models a relationship between two quantities, interpret key features of graphs and tables in terms of the quantities, and sketch graphs showing key features given a verbal description of the relationship. Key features include: intercepts; intervals where the function is increasing, decreasing, positive, or negative; relative maximums and minimums; symmetries; end behavior; and periodicity.

A32.title: Comparing Linear Functions in Different Representations | Algebra 1 Worksheet
A32.ican: compare two functions' rates of change and initial values when they are shown in different forms.
A32.key_rule: Find the same feature in each function, then compare: a rate needs two points; an initial value is the output at x = 0.
A32.key_rule_hint: Changes faster means the bigger size of the change in y for each 1 in x, whichever way it goes.

watch.text: A: y = 4x − 1. B has the pairs (0, 1), (1, 4), (2, 7). Which has the greater rate of change?
watch.wrong: B's rate is 4, from (1, 4): the same as A
watch.wrong_why: 4 is one y-value, not a change.
watch.right_why: A rate needs two points.

A32.learn: Students learn to find the rate of change and the initial value of a function given as a rule, a table, a graph or words, and compare two functions feature by feature.
A32.watchout: a wrong and a right rate comparison of y = 4x − 1 and a table with (0, 1), (1, 4), (2, 7); the wrong one reads the y-value 4 as the table's rate.
mistakes: Reads one y-value as the rate of change
Swaps the rate of change and the initial value
Compares initial values when the question asks about rates
Forgets to divide the change in y by the change in x
Reads a minus sign in the rule as a decreasing function

standards.text: Compare properties of two functions each represented in a different way (algebraically, graphically, numerically in tables, or by verbal descriptions). For example, given a graph of one quadratic function and an algebraic expression for another, say which has the larger maximum.

A33.skill: Piecewise, Step, and Absolute Value Functions
A33.title: Piecewise Functions | Evaluating Step & Absolute Value Functions | Algebra 1
A33.ican: use the right piece of a piecewise, step, or absolute value function, and read its open and closed circles.
A33.key_rule: Find the piece whose x-values hold your x, then use only that rule. At a break, the closed circle counts.
A33.key_rule_hint: Which piece is drawn or written first does not matter; the circle does.

watch.text: g(x) = x + 4 for x < 2, and g(x) = 1 for x ≥ 2. Find g(2).
watch.wrong_why: x + 4 is only for x < 2, and 2 is not less than 2.
watch.right_why: The ≥ piece holds x = 2: its closed circle counts.

A33.learn: Students learn to find the piece whose x-values hold an input and use only its rule, read open and closed circles at a break, and find the vertex and values of an absolute value function.
A33.watchout: a wrong and a right g(2) for a two-piece function with g(x) = 1 when x ≥ 2; the wrong one uses the x < 2 piece, x + 4, and gets 6.
mistakes: Uses the wrong piece or the open circle at a break point
Leaves the value of an absolute value negative
Puts the vertex of |x + 2| at x = 2
Reads under as including the boundary, or lets two pieces share an endpoint

standards.text: Graph square root, cube root, and piecewise-defined functions, including step functions and absolute value functions.

A34.skill: Rate of Change and Slope from a Graph
A34.title: Finding Slope from a Graph | Rise Over Run & Rate of Change | Algebra 1 Notes
A34.ican: find a line's slope by counting the rise and the run between two grid corners.
A34.key_rule: Count left to right: slope = rise ÷ run, with the rise on top. Write the simplest fraction.
A34.key_rule_hint: Steeper means a slope farther from 0, whichever sign it has.

watch.text: A line rises 3 units for every 7 units it runs to the right. What is its slope?
watch.wrong_why: The bigger number went on top: that is run over rise.
watch.right_why: Rise over run: the rise goes on top.

A34.learn: Students learn to count the rise and the run between two grid corners on a line, write the slope as rise over run in simplest form with the right sign, and give a rate of change with its units.
A34.watchout: a wrong and a right slope for a line that rises 3 units for every 7 units it runs side by side; the wrong one writes run over rise, 7/3, instead of 3/7.
mistakes: Puts the run on top instead of the rise
Drops the minus sign of a falling line
Judges steepness by the sign of the slope instead of its size
Mixes up a slope of 0 and an undefined slope

standards.text: Calculate and interpret the average rate of change of a function (presented symbolically or as a table) over a specified interval. Estimate the rate of change from a graph.

A35.title: Slope Formula Worksheet | Finding Slope from Two Points | Algebra 1 Notes & Key
A35.ican: find the slope through two points, subtracting in the same order on top and bottom.
A35.key_rule: Subtract in the same order on top and bottom. Put a negative number in ( ), then simplify.
A35.key_rule_hint: Swapping the order on only one of them flips the sign.

watch.text: Find the slope of the line through (2, 9) and (6, 1).
watch.wrong_why: The top starts at (6, 1); the bottom starts at (2, 9).
watch.right_why: Start both from (6, 1).

A35.learn: Students learn to find the slope through two points with (y₂ − y₁) ÷ (x₂ − x₁), in the same order on top and bottom, and tell a slope of 0 from an undefined one.
A35.watchout: a wrong and a right slope through (2, 9) and (6, 1) side by side; the wrong one starts the top and the bottom from different points and gets 2 instead of −2.
mistakes: Starts the top and the bottom of the slope formula from different points
Subtracts a negative coordinate as if it were positive
Puts the change in x on top
Calls a slope with 0 in the denominator 0 instead of undefined

standards.text: Calculate and interpret the average rate of change of a function (presented symbolically or as a table) over a specified interval. Estimate the rate of change from a graph.

A36.title: Graphing Slope-Intercept Form | Graphing Linear Equations Worksheet | Algebra 1
A36.ican: graph y = mx + b by plotting (0, b) first, then stepping by the slope.
A36.key_rule: Plot (0, b) first, then step by m to a second point, and draw the line through both.
A36.key_rule_hint: Step from (0, b), never from the origin unless b = 0.
A36.key_formula: start (0, b), then step by m

watch.text: Kim graphs y = 3x + 2 by starting at the origin and stepping up 3, right 1.
watch.wrong_why: That line crosses the y-axis at 0, not at 2.
watch.right_why: Start at b, then step by m.

A36.learn: Students learn to read m and b from y = mx + b (rewriting it first when needed), plot (0, b), step by the slope to a second point and draw the line.
A36.watchout: a wrong and a right graph of y = 3x + 2 side by side; the wrong one starts at the origin and steps to (1, 3) instead of starting at (0, 2).
mistakes: Reads m and b in the order they are written instead of by role
Steps up for a negative slope
Drops the sign of b
Starts the graph at the origin instead of at (0, b)
Divides only one term when solving for y

standards.text: Graph linear and quadratic functions and show intercepts, maxima, and minima.

A37.title: Writing Linear Equations in Slope-Intercept Form Worksheet | Algebra 1 Notes
A37.ican: write y = mx + b by reading b off the y-axis and finding m.
A37.key_rule: Find the slope m, then b, the value of y when x is 0. The x-axis crossing is never read as b.
A37.key_rule_hint: Both crossings are on the graph; b is the one on the y-axis.

watch.text: A line has slope 1/2. It crosses the x-axis at 6 and the y-axis at −3. Lee writes its equation.
watch.wrong_why: 6 is the x-axis crossing.
watch.right_why: b is read off the y-axis only.

A37.learn: Students learn to write y = mx + b from a slope and a point, two points, a graph or a story, with b read off the y-axis.
A37.watchout: a wrong and a right equation for a line with slope 1/2 that crosses the x-axis at 6 and the y-axis at −3; the wrong one uses the x-axis crossing as b.
mistakes: Reads b off the x-axis instead of the y-axis
Swaps the slope and the y-intercept
Uses a point's y-value as b
Gives a falling line a positive slope

standards.text: Create equations in two or more variables to represent relationships between quantities; graph equations on coordinate axes with labels and scales.

A38.title: Writing Equations in Point-Slope Form Worksheet | Algebra 1 Notes & Answer Key
A38.ican: write a line in point-slope form from one point and the slope.
A38.key_rule: Put the point into y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) and keep the subtraction: a negative coordinate comes out as a plus.

watch.text: Write the line with slope 2 through (5, −3) in point-slope form.
watch.wrong_why: That uses y₁ = 3, not −3.

A38.learn: Students learn to write y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) from a point and the slope, turning a negative coordinate into a plus.
A38.watchout: a wrong and a right point-slope equation for slope 2 through (5, −3) side by side; the wrong one writes y − 3 instead of y + 3.
mistakes: Copies the sign of a negative y-coordinate instead of subtracting it
Copies the sign of a negative x-coordinate instead of subtracting it
Swaps the x- and y-coordinates of the point
Drops the sign of a slope found from two points

standards.text: Create equations in two or more variables to represent relationships between quantities; graph equations on coordinate axes with labels and scales.

A39.skill: Standard Form and Graphing with Intercepts
A39.title: Finding X and Y Intercepts Worksheet | Graphing Standard Form | Algebra 1 Notes
A39.ican: find both intercepts of Ax + By = C and graph the line through them.
A39.key_rule: Set the other variable to 0. Don't stop at C: divide it by the coefficient left.
A39.key_rule_hint: 2x + 7y = 14 crosses the y-axis at 2, not at 14.

watch.text: Find the y-intercept of 3x + 5y = 30.
watch.wrong_why: 30 is C, the total; nothing was divided.
watch.right_why: Set x = 0, then divide by 5.

A39.learn: Students learn to find the intercepts of Ax + By = C by setting the other variable to 0, write them as points and graph the line through them.
A39.watchout: a wrong and a right y-intercept of 3x + 5y = 30 side by side; the wrong one gives 30, the constant, instead of setting x = 0 to get (0, 6).
mistakes: Reads the constant C as an intercept
Drops the sign of a negative y coefficient
Writes an intercept's coordinates in the wrong order
Graphs from one intercept only, or through the constant

standards.text: Create equations in two or more variables to represent relationships between quantities; graph equations on coordinate axes with labels and scales.

A40.skill: Converting Between Forms of Linear Equations
A40.title: Converting Forms of Linear Equations | Standard to Slope-Intercept | Algebra 1
A40.ican: rewrite a linear equation in another form without changing the line.
A40.key_rule: Changing the form never changes the line: do the same to every term, then check one point in both.
A40.key_rule_hint: Put the same x into both forms: they must give the same y.
A40.key_formula: y = mx + b ↔ Ax + By = C

watch.text: Write y = (3/4)x − 2 in standard form.
watch.wrong_why: The −2 was not multiplied by 4.
watch.right_why: Multiply every term by 4.

A40.learn: Students learn to rewrite a line in another form by doing the same to every term, then test one point in both forms.
A40.watchout: a wrong and a right conversion of y = (3/4)x − 2 to standard form side by side; the wrong one does not multiply the −2 by 4 and gets 3x − 4y = 2.
mistakes: Forgets to multiply the constant when clearing a fraction
Divides only the x term when solving for y
Moves a term to the other side with the wrong sign
Leaves the x coefficient negative in standard form

standards.text: Use the structure of an expression to identify ways to rewrite it. For example, see x⁴ - y⁴ as (x²)² - (y²)², thus recognizing it as a difference of squares that can be factored as (x² - y²)(x² + y²).

A41.title: Parallel and Perpendicular Lines Worksheet | Slopes of Lines | Algebra 1 Notes
A41.ican: use slopes to tell whether two lines are parallel, perpendicular or neither.
A41.key_rule: Parallel lines have the same slope; perpendicular slopes are opposite reciprocals, so their product is −1.
A41.key_rule_hint: Every line on this sheet can be written y = mx + b: none is vertical.

watch.text: Find the slope of a line perpendicular to y = (3/4)x − 2.
watch.wrong_why: Only the sign changed; 3/4 was not flipped.
watch.right_why: Flip and change the sign: the product is −1.

A41.learn: Students learn to compare slopes to tell parallel, perpendicular or neither, and write a parallel or perpendicular line through a point.
A41.watchout: a wrong and a right perpendicular slope to y = (3/4)x − 2 side by side; the wrong one only changes the sign to −3/4 instead of flipping to −4/3.
mistakes: Changes only the sign for a perpendicular slope
Flips the slope but keeps its sign
Calls slopes with opposite signs perpendicular
Keeps the old y-intercept for the new line instead of using the point

standards.text: Prove the slope criteria for parallel and perpendicular lines and use them to solve geometric problems (e.g., find the equation of a line parallel or perpendicular to a given line that passes through a given point).

A42.title: Direct Variation Worksheet | Constant of Variation | Algebra 1 Notes & Key
A42.ican: test y ÷ x on every pair to tell direct variation and find k.
A42.key_rule: Direct variation is y = kx: y ÷ x is the same for every pair, and the line passes through the origin.
A42.key_rule_hint: A straight line that misses (0, 0) is not direct variation.

watch.text: Ana calls y = 2x + 3 direct variation because its graph is a straight line.
watch.wrong_why: Straight is not enough; nothing may be added.
watch.right_why: The ratio moves, and the line misses (0, 0).

A42.learn: Students learn to divide y by x for every pair to tell whether a relationship is direct variation, then write y = kx.
A42.watchout: a wrong and a right answer to whether y = 2x + 3 is direct variation side by side; the wrong one says yes because the graph is straight, but y ÷ x changes.
mistakes: Calls any straight line direct variation
Divides x by y to find k
Checks only some of the pairs in a table
Adds instead of multiplying by k to predict a value

standards.text: Create equations in two or more variables to represent relationships between quantities; graph equations on coordinate axes with labels and scales.

A43.skill: Writing Linear Models from Tables and Contexts
A43.title: Writing Linear Equations from Word Problems & Tables | Linear Models | Algebra 1
A43.ican: write y = mx + b from a table or a story and test it on every row.
A43.key_rule: Find m as the change in y ÷ the change in x, then b from one point; the model must fit every row.
A43.key_rule_hint: A table's first y is b only when its x is 0.

watch.text: A table has (2, 11), (4, 17) and (6, 23). Sam writes its model.
watch.wrong_why: 11 is y at x = 2, not at x = 0.
watch.right_why: Find b from a row; then every row fits.

A43.learn: Students learn to find the rate from two rows, find b from one row, write y = mx + b, then test the model on every row or fact.
A43.watchout: a wrong and a right model for a table with (2, 11), (4, 17), (6, 23) side by side; the wrong one uses 11 as b, but 11 is y at x = 2.
mistakes: Takes the first y-value in a table as b
Takes the first reading in a story as the starting value
Uses the change in y as the rate without dividing by the x change
Swaps the rate and the one-time amount, or drops the sign of a decrease

standards.text: Determine an explicit expression, a recursive process, or steps for calculation from a context.

A44.skill: Interpreting Slope and Intercept in Context
A44.title: Interpreting Slope and Y-Intercept in Context Worksheet | Algebra 1 Notes & Key
A44.ican: say what the slope and the intercept mean in a story, with units.
A44.key_rule: The slope is a rate, said with the word per; the intercept is the value of y at x = 0, with the y-unit.
A44.key_rule_hint: A slope said without a rate word sounds like one amount.

watch.text: A phone plan costs y = 15x + 20 dollars for x GB. Kim reads the slope.
watch.wrong_why: $15 alone is one amount, not a rate.
watch.right_why: A slope is a rate: say per and both units.

A44.learn: Students learn to say the slope as a rate with per and two units, and the intercept as the value at x = 0 with one unit.
A44.watchout: a wrong and a right reading of the slope of y = 15x + 20 dollars for x GB side by side; the wrong one says $15 instead of $15 per GB.
mistakes: Says the slope as one amount with no per
Reads the slope as the starting value
Reads the intercept as a rate
Drops the direction of a negative slope
Trusts an intercept whose x = 0 does not fit the story

standards.text: Interpret the parameters in a linear or exponential function in terms of a context.

A45.title: Transformations of Linear Functions | Function Transformations | Algebra 1 Notes
A45.ican: write a shifted, stretched or flipped line and tell which way it moves.
A45.key_rule: A number added outside f( ) moves the graph up or down; a number added inside moves it left or right, the opposite way to its sign.
A45.key_rule_hint: For a left/right shift, test a point: if g(6) gives what f(0) gave, the shift is right 6.

watch.text: f(x) = x + 5. A student says g(x) = f(x − 4) moves the graph left 4.
watch.wrong_why: The sign inside works on the input, not the direction.
watch.right_why: x must be 4 bigger to give the same output.

A45.learn: Students learn to write g(x) from f(x) for a shift, stretch or flip, and test a point to tell which way the graph moves.
A45.watchout: a wrong and a right reading of g(x) = f(x − 4) side by side; the wrong one moves the graph left 4 because of the minus, but it moves right 4.
mistakes: Reads a minus inside the parentheses as a shift left
Multiplies only the slope when stretching every output
Calls a change in slope a shift
Lets a minus in front reach only the first term

standards.text: Identify the effect on the graph of replacing f(x) by f(x) + k, k f(x), f(kx), and f(x + k) for specific values of k (both positive and negative); find the value of k given the graphs. Experiment with cases and illustrate an explanation of the effects on the graph using technology. Include recognizing even and odd functions from their graphs and algebraic expressions for them.

A46.title: Solving Linear Equations by Graphing Worksheet | Algebra 1 Notes & Answer Key
A46.ican: solve an equation by graphing both sides and reading the x where they cross.
A46.key_rule: Go straight up or down from the crossing to the x-axis: that x is the solution. Then check it in both sides.
A46.key_rule_hint: The y-value tells what both sides equal; the equation asked for x.

watch.text: Graphed, the sides of 2x + 1 = x + 4 cross at (3, 7). A student says x = 7.
watch.wrong_why: 7 is what both sides equal, not the input.
watch.right_why: The solution is the crossing's x.

A46.learn: Students learn to solve an equation by graphing each side as a line and reading the x of the crossing, then test it in both sides.
A46.watchout: a wrong and a right answer for 2x + 1 = x + 4, whose graphed sides cross at (3, 7); the wrong one gives the crossing's y-value, x = 7, not x = 3.
mistakes: Answers with the crossing's y-value instead of its x-value
Swaps the x- and y-coordinates of the crossing
Gives the whole point as the solution of a one-variable equation
Stops before finding the y-value of the crossing point

standards.text: Explain why the x-coordinates of the points where the graphs of the equations y = f(x) and y = g(x) intersect are the solutions of the equation f(x) = g(x); find the solutions approximately, e.g., using technology to graph the functions, make tables of values, or find successive approximations. Include cases where f(x) and/or g(x) are linear, polynomial, rational, absolute value, exponential, and logarithmic functions.

A47.title: Solving Systems of Equations by Graphing Worksheet | Algebra 1 Notes & Key
A47.ican: solve a system by graphing both lines and naming the point where they cross.
A47.key_rule: The solution is the whole point where the lines cross; check it in both equations.
A47.key_rule_hint: A system has two letters, so its solution has two numbers.

watch.text: The lines y = x + 4 and y = −x − 2 cross at (−3, 1). A student says x = −3.
watch.wrong_why: Only the x; the y is missing.
watch.right_why: A system in x and y needs both numbers.

A47.learn: Students learn to solve a system by graphing both lines, name the crossing as a point (x, y), and test it in both equations.
A47.watchout: a wrong and a right answer for y = x + 4 and y = −x − 2, which cross at (−3, 1); the wrong one gives only x = −3 instead of the point.
mistakes: Gives only the x-value as the solution of a system
Checks the point in one equation and stops
Swaps the coordinates of the crossing point
Finds x but not y

standards.text: Solve systems of linear equations exactly and approximately (e.g., with graphs), focusing on pairs of linear equations in two variables.

A48.title: Solving Systems of Equations by Substitution Worksheet | Algebra 1 Notes & Key
A48.ican: solve a system by putting one equation's expression into the other and finding both values.
A48.key_rule: Put the expression in parentheses into the other equation; find both values, then check the point in both.
A48.key_rule_hint: A minus in front of ( ) changes the sign of every term inside.

watch.text: For 3x − y = 5 and y = x + 1, a student writes 3x − x + 1 = 5.
watch.wrong_why: The minus reached only the x.
watch.right_why: In ( ), the minus reaches both terms: 2x − 1 = 5.

A48.learn: Students learn to solve a system by substituting an expression in parentheses into the other equation, then find both values and test the point.
A48.watchout: a wrong and a right substitution of y = x + 1 into 3x − y = 5 side by side; the wrong one drops the parentheses, so the minus reaches only the x.
mistakes: Drops the parentheses, so a minus reaches only the first term
Writes the coordinates in the order they were found
Substitutes the expression back into its own equation
Checks only the equation the expression came from

standards.text: Solve systems of linear equations exactly and approximately (e.g., with graphs), focusing on pairs of linear equations in two variables.

A49.title: Solving Systems of Equations by Elimination Worksheet | Algebra 1 Notes & Key
A49.ican: solve a system by adding or subtracting the equations to eliminate a variable.
A49.key_rule: Make one letter's coefficients opposites and add; to set them up, multiply a whole equation, the constant too.
A49.key_rule_hint: Equal coefficients cancel by subtracting instead; adding equal terms doubles them.

watch.text: For x + 3y = 10 and 2x + y = 15, a student multiplies the second equation by 3.
watch.wrong_why: The 3 never reached the 15.
watch.right_why: Every term, both sides: 3(15) = 45.

A49.learn: Students learn to solve a system by adding or subtracting the equations so one letter cancels, multiplying a whole equation first when needed.
A49.watchout: a wrong and a right way to multiply 2x + y = 15 by 3 side by side; the wrong one writes 6x + 3y = 15, leaving the constant unmultiplied.
mistakes: Multiplies only the left side of an equation
Subtracts the left sides one way and the right sides the other
Adds equal terms and drops the variable anyway
Checks only the equation used to find the second value

standards.text: Prove that, given a system of two equations in two variables, replacing one equation by the sum of that equation and a multiple of the other produces a system with the same solutions.

A50.skill: Choosing a Method and Special Systems
A50.title: Solving Systems of Equations Worksheet | Special Systems | Algebra 1 Notes & Key
A50.ican: decide which method fits a system, and tell no solution from infinitely many.
A50.key_rule: If every letter cancels, a false statement means no solution; a true one means infinitely many: the points on the one line.
A50.key_rule_hint: Infinitely many is not every ordered pair: test a pair in both equations.

watch.text: For 2x + y = 7 and 4x + 2y = 6, a student doubles the first equation, subtracts and gets 0 = 8.
watch.wrong_why: The letters cancelled, but 0 = 8 is false.
watch.right_why: Parallel lines: no pair fits both.

A50.learn: Students learn to pick a method that fits a system, and read a false statement as no solution and a true one as infinitely many solutions.
A50.watchout: a wrong and a right reading of 0 = 8 from 2x + y = 7 and 4x + 2y = 6; the wrong one says infinitely many, but a false statement means no solution.
mistakes: Reads a true statement such as 0 = 0 as no solution
Reads a false statement as infinitely many solutions
Takes infinitely many solutions to mean any ordered pair works
Graphs a system whose crossing point is not on a gridline

standards.text: Solve systems of linear equations exactly and approximately (e.g., with graphs), focusing on pairs of linear equations in two variables.

A51.title: Systems of Equations Word Problems Worksheet | Writing Systems | Algebra 1 Notes
A51.ican: write a system from a context, name what the letters mean, and solve it.
A51.key_rule: Write one equation per fact, dollars equal to dollars; solve, answer in words, then check in the story.
A51.key_rule_hint: Read each side aloud with its unit: tickets = tickets, dollars = dollars.

watch.text: 9 items cost $66: shirts (x) $9 each, hats (y) $6 each. A student writes the dollar fact.
watch.wrong_why: Dollars on the left, items on the right.
watch.right_why: Dollars on both sides: $66.

A51.learn: Students learn to define both variables with units, write one equation per fact, solve, and answer in words with units.
A51.watchout: a wrong and a right equation for 9 items costing $66, shirts at $9 and hats at $6; the wrong one writes 9x + 6y = 9, mixing dollars and items.
mistakes: Writes an equation with different units on its two sides
Reports the right numbers against the wrong labels
Uses x + y for a perimeter instead of 2x + 2y
Stops after finding one value

standards.text: Represent constraints by equations or inequalities, and by systems of equations and/or inequalities, and interpret solutions as viable or nonviable options in a modeling context. For example, represent inequalities describing nutritional and cost constraints on combinations of different foods.

A52.title: Arithmetic Sequences Worksheet | Arithmetic Sequence Formula | Algebra 1 Notes
A52.ican: write the rule for an arithmetic sequence and use it to find any term.
A52.key_rule: Term n sits n − 1 steps after a₁: multiply d by n − 1, not by n, and test the rule at n = 1.
A52.key_rule_hint: A correct rule gives back the first term when n = 1.

watch.text: For 4, 9, 14, 19, ... a student writes the rule aₙ = 4 + 5n.
watch.wrong_why: At n = 1 it gives 9, the second term.
watch.right_why: At n = 1: 4 + 5(0) = 4, the first term.

A52.learn: Students learn to find the common difference, write aₙ = a₁ + d(n − 1), and use it to find a term or which term has a value.
A52.watchout: a wrong and a right rule for the sequence 4, 9, 14, 19 side by side; the wrong one writes aₙ = 4 + 5n, which gives 9 at n = 1.
mistakes: Multiplies the common difference by n instead of n − 1
Gives the number of steps instead of the term number
Adds before multiplying when finding a term
Divides by the term number instead of the number of steps to find d

standards.text: Write arithmetic and geometric sequences both recursively and with an explicit formula, use them to model situations, and translate between the two forms.

A53.title: Geometric Sequences Worksheet | Arithmetic and Geometric Sequences | Algebra 1
A53.ican: find the common ratio of a geometric sequence and write a rule for any term.
A53.key_rule: Find r by dividing a term by the one before, not by subtracting, and check a second pair.
A53.key_rule_hint: A difference that changes from pair to pair is not an arithmetic rule.

watch.text: For 2, 10, 50, 250, ... a student subtracts to find the rule.
watch.wrong_why: 50 − 10 = 40, not 8: the gap changes.
watch.right_why: Dividing gives 5 on both pairs.

A53.learn: Students learn to divide to find the common ratio r, test a second pair, and use aₙ = a₁ · rⁿ⁻¹ to find any term.
A53.watchout: a wrong and a right rule for the sequence 2, 10, 50, 250 side by side; the wrong one subtracts and says add 8, but dividing gives the ratio 5.
mistakes: Subtracts instead of dividing to find the common ratio
Uses n factors of r instead of n − 1
Stops at r³ instead of taking the cube root
Loses the sign of a negative common ratio
Makes an even power of a negative ratio negative

standards.text: Write arithmetic and geometric sequences both recursively and with an explicit formula, use them to model situations, and translate between the two forms.

A54.skill: Sequences as Functions: Recursive and Explicit
A54.title: Explicit and Recursive Formulas Worksheet | Sequences as Functions | Algebra 1
A54.ican: write recursive and explicit rules for a sequence and treat it as a function of n.
A54.key_rule: A recursive rule needs a first term as well as the step; an explicit rule jumps straight to term n.
A54.key_rule_hint: A sequence's graph is dots at n = 1, 2, 3 and so on, never a joined line.

watch.text: A student writes aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + 4 and calls it a whole sequence.
watch.right_why: The first term picks one sequence.

A54.learn: Students learn to write a recursive rule with its first term, turn it into an explicit rule, and graph a sequence as separate dots.
A54.watchout: a wrong and a right recursive rule side by side; the wrong one gives only aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + 4 with no first term, so many sequences fit it.
mistakes: Gives a recursive rule with no first term
Reads aₙ₋₁ as the number n − 1 instead of the previous term
Accepts a term number that is not a positive integer
Adds the common difference n times instead of n − 1

standards.text: Recognize that sequences are functions, sometimes defined recursively, whose domain is a subset of the integers. For example, the Fibonacci sequence is defined recursively by f(0) = f(1) = 1, f(n+1) = f(n) + f(n-1) for n ≥ 1.

A55.title: Exponent Rules Worksheet | Laws & Properties of Exponents | Algebra 1 Notes
A55.ican: use the exponent rules for products, powers and quotients, and explain each by counting factors.
A55.key_rule: Keep the base and add the exponents when you multiply; if a rule slips your mind, write the factors out and count.
A55.key_rule_hint: Simplest form: one number, each letter once. No variable on this sheet is 0.

watch.text: A student multiplies the exponents in x³ · x⁴.
watch.wrong_why: 3 × 4 is the rule for (x³)⁴.
watch.right_why: Three x's and four x's make seven x's.

A55.learn: Students learn to multiply, divide and raise powers of one base by counting factors, with the coefficients worked as numbers.
A55.watchout: a wrong and a right product of x³ · x⁴ side by side; the wrong one multiplies the exponents to get x¹², which is the rule for (x³)⁴, instead of x⁷.
mistakes: Multiplies the exponents when powers of one base are multiplied
Multiplies the bases as well as adding the exponents
Leaves the coefficient out when raising a product to a power
Drops the coefficient in a quotient

standards.text: Explain how the definition of the meaning of rational exponents follows from extending the properties of integer exponents to those values, allowing for a notation for radicals in terms of rational exponents. For example, we define 5^(1/3) to be the cube root of 5 because we want (5^(1/3))³ = 5^((1/3)3) to hold, so (5^(1/3))³ must equal 5.

A56.title: Zero and Negative Exponents Worksheet | Integer Exponents | Algebra 1 Notes
A56.ican: rewrite zero and negative exponents correctly and write answers with positive exponents.
A56.key_rule: A negative exponent flips the power to the other side of the fraction bar; it never changes the sign.
A56.key_rule_hint: No variable on this sheet is 0, so x⁰ and x⁻² always make sense.

watch.text: A student reads the minus in x⁻² as a negative sign.
watch.wrong_why: At x = 3: 3⁻² is 1/9, but −3² is −9.
watch.right_why: At x = 3 it gives 1/9, a positive number.

A56.learn: Students learn to use x⁰ = 1 and x⁻ⁿ = 1/xⁿ for nonzero x, and write every answer with positive exponents only.
A56.watchout: a wrong and a right meaning of x⁻² side by side; the wrong one reads the minus as a negative sign, −x², instead of 1/x².
mistakes: Reads a negative exponent as a negative number
Loses the sign of an even power of a negative base
Moves the coefficient along with the variable that has the negative exponent
Applies a zero exponent to the coefficient in front

standards.text: Explain how the definition of the meaning of rational exponents follows from extending the properties of integer exponents to those values, allowing for a notation for radicals in terms of rational exponents. For example, we define 5^(1/3) to be the cube root of 5 because we want (5^(1/3))³ = 5^((1/3)3) to hold, so (5^(1/3))³ must equal 5.

A57.title: Rational Exponents and Radicals Worksheet | Fractional Exponents | Algebra 1
A57.ican: move between rational exponents and radical form without swapping the root and the power.
A57.key_rule: In a rational exponent, the bottom number is the root and the top number is the power.
A57.key_rule_hint: Every base on this sheet is positive. In ³√x the small 3 is the index; √ covers the number or letter right after it, or everything in the ( ) after it.

watch.text: A student reads 64²ᐟ³ as a square root, then a cube.
watch.wrong_why: The 2 is on top, so it is the power, not the root.
watch.right_why: The bottom 3 is the root: ³√64 = 4, and 4² = 16.

A57.learn: Students learn to read the bottom number of a rational exponent as the root and the top number as the power, and write roots and rational exponents either way.
A57.watchout: a wrong and a right evaluation of 64²ᐟ³ side by side; the wrong one takes a square root and then cubes, getting 512, instead of (³√64)² = 16.
mistakes: Swaps the root and the power in a rational exponent
Reads a fractional exponent as division of the base
Reads the index of a root as a power
Reads a negative exponent as a negative number

standards.text: Explain how the definition of the meaning of rational exponents follows from extending the properties of integer exponents to those values, allowing for a notation for radicals in terms of rational exponents. For example, we define 5^(1/3) to be the cube root of 5 because we want (5^(1/3))³ = 5^((1/3)3) to hold, so (5^(1/3))³ must equal 5.
Rewrite expressions involving radicals and rational exponents using the properties of exponents.

A58.title: Simplifying Radicals Worksheet | Simplifying Square Roots | Algebra 1 Notes
A58.ican: simplify a square root by its largest perfect square factor, and add before taking a root of a sum.
A58.key_rule: Write the radicand as the largest perfect square factor times what is left, then take the square's root.
A58.key_rule_hint: Under a plus sign, add first. Every letter on this sheet is positive; √ covers the number or letter right after it, or everything in the ( ) after it.

watch.text: A student splits √(9 + 16) over the plus sign.
watch.wrong_why: A root does not split over a plus sign.
watch.right_why: Add first, then take the root.

A58.learn: Students learn to write a square root in simplest radical form by splitting off its largest perfect square factor, and to add first under a plus sign.
A58.watchout: a wrong and a right simplification of √(9 + 16) side by side; the wrong one splits the root over the plus sign to get 7 instead of √25 = 5.
mistakes: Splits a square root over a plus sign
Brings a perfect square out without taking its root
Drops the number already in front of the radical
Stops at a perfect square factor that is not the largest
Takes a variable power out of the radical whole instead of its root

standards.text: Rewrite expressions involving radicals and rational exponents using the properties of exponents.

A59.title: Operations with Radicals | Adding, Subtracting & Multiplying Radicals Algebra 1
A59.ican: add and subtract like radicals, multiply radicals, and simplify every result.
A59.key_rule: Only radicals with the same radicand combine into one term when added or subtracted; multiplying puts the radicands together under one √.
A59.key_rule_hint: Simplify every radical first: radicals that look unlike may match. 2√3 + 3√5 stays as it is.

watch.text: A student adds 2√3 + 3√5 by adding everything.
