watch.wrong_why: √3 and √5 are unlike, so they do not combine.
watch.right_why: Unlike radicals stay apart: 2√3 + 3√5 is finished.

A59.learn: Students learn to simplify each radical, add or subtract only radicals with the same radicand, multiply by joining the radicands, and finish in simplest radical form.
A59.watchout: a wrong and a right look at 2√3 + 3√5 side by side; the wrong one adds everything to get 5√8, but unlike radicals do not combine.
mistakes: Adds or subtracts the radicands along with the coefficients
Adds the radicands when multiplying radicals
Stops before simplifying a product
Calls radicals unlike before simplifying each one

standards.text: Rewrite expressions involving radicals and rational exponents using the properties of exponents.

A60.title: Operations with Scientific Notation Worksheet | Multiplying & Dividing Algebra 1
A60.ican: multiply and divide in scientific notation and adjust the answer so its coefficient is at least 1 and less than 10.
A60.key_rule: When the coefficient is divided by 10, the exponent goes up by 1; when it is multiplied by 10, the exponent goes down by 1.
A60.key_rule_hint: Adjust until the coefficient is at least 1 and less than 10; the value never changes. To add, match the exponents first.

watch.text: A student adjusts 30 × 10⁻⁵ and writes 3 × 10⁻⁶.
watch.wrong_why: Both parts got smaller: the value is now 100 times too small.
watch.right_why: 30 went down to 3, so the exponent goes up: −5 + 1 = −4.

A60.learn: Students learn to multiply and divide numbers in scientific notation, then adjust the coefficient and move the exponent the other way, so the value stays the same.
A60.watchout: a wrong and a right adjustment of 30 × 10⁻⁵ side by side; the wrong one writes 3 × 10⁻⁶, shrinking both parts, instead of 3 × 10⁻⁴.
mistakes: Moves the coefficient and the exponent the same way
Leaves a coefficient of 10 or more unadjusted
Subtracts a negative exponent as if it were positive
Squares only the power of 10
Adds before matching the exponents

standards.text: Use units as a way to understand problems and to guide the solution of multi-step problems; choose and interpret units consistently in formulas; choose and interpret the scale and the origin in graphs and data displays.

A61.title: Graphing Exponential Functions Worksheet | Algebra 1 Notes, Slides & Answer Key
A61.ican: graph an exponential function from a table and give its y-intercept, asymptote, domain and range.
A61.key_rule: Each step left divides by b. That never reaches 0, so bˣ is positive for every x.
A61.key_rule_hint: Every function y = a · bˣ on this sheet has a > 0: domain all real numbers, range y > 0, no x-intercept.
A61.key_formula: y = a · bˣ: (0, a); asymptote y = 0

watch.text: A student graphs y = 3ˣ and says it meets the x-axis at x = −4.
watch.wrong_why: 3⁻⁴ is small, but it is not 0.
watch.right_why: A positive base to any power is positive.

A61.learn: Students learn to make a table for y = a · bˣ, graph it, and explain why the curve gets closer and closer to the x-axis but never touches it.
A61.watchout: a wrong and a right reading of y = 3ˣ at x = −4 side by side; the wrong one says the graph meets the x-axis there, but 3⁻⁴ = 1/81 is not 0.
mistakes: Calls a small positive value 0, so the curve meets the x-axis
Uses the base as the y-intercept
Puts 0 in the range of an exponential function
Reads a negative exponent as a negative number
Keeps y = 0 as the asymptote after the graph is shifted up

standards.text: Graph exponential and logarithmic functions, showing intercepts and end behavior, and trigonometric functions, showing period, midline, and amplitude.

A62.title: Exponential Growth Worksheet | Growth Models & Formula | Algebra 1 Notes & Key
A62.ican: write an exponential growth model from a percent rate and read the rate back from the factor.
A62.key_rule: The factor is 1 + r, never r alone: the 1 keeps what you had and the r adds the increase.
A62.key_rule_hint: Keep the factor exact and round only the final answer.

watch.text: For 4% growth a year on 600, a student writes y = 600(0.04)ᵗ.
watch.wrong_why: At t = 1 it gives 600 × 0.04 = 24: it shrank.
watch.right_why: The factor is 1 + 0.04, so 600 grows to 624 in a year.

A62.learn: Students learn to turn a growth rate into the factor 1 + r, write y = a(1 + r)ᵗ, use it after t periods, and read the rate back from a factor.
A62.watchout: a wrong and a right model for 4% yearly growth on 600 side by side; the wrong one uses the rate as the factor, y = 600(0.04)ᵗ, instead of y = 600(1.04)ᵗ.
mistakes: Uses the growth rate as the factor instead of 1 + r
Reads the growth factor as the rate
Rounds the growth factor before using it
Adds the same amount each period instead of multiplying
Reads a factor such as 1.006 as 6% growth instead of 0.6%

standards.text: Construct linear and exponential functions, including arithmetic and geometric sequences, given a graph, a description of a relationship, or two input-output pairs (include reading these from a table).

A63.title: Exponential Decay Worksheet | Decay Models & Formula | Algebra 1 Notes & Key
A63.ican: write an exponential decay model from a percent rate and read the rate back from the factor.
A63.key_rule: The decay factor is 1 − r, the part left after each period, and it is always between 0 and 1.
A63.key_rule_hint: 8% lost means 92% kept. Keep the factor exact and round only the final answer.

watch.text: For 10% decay a year on 500, a student writes y = 500(−0.1)ᵗ.
watch.wrong_why: It gives −50, then 5: the sign flips.

A63.learn: Students learn to turn a decay rate into the factor 1 − r, write y = a(1 − r)ᵗ, use it after t periods, and read the rate back from a factor.
A63.watchout: a wrong and a right model for 10% yearly decay on 500 side by side; the wrong one uses a negative base, y = 500(−0.1)ᵗ, instead of y = 500(0.9)ᵗ.
mistakes: Uses a negative base for decay
Uses the part lost as the factor instead of the part kept
Reads the part kept as the decay rate
Finds 1 − r by moving the decimal point instead of subtracting
Calls a factor greater than 1 decay
Takes the same amount off each period

standards.text: Construct linear and exponential functions, including arithmetic and geometric sequences, given a graph, a description of a relationship, or two input-output pairs (include reading these from a table).

A64.title: Compound Interest Worksheet | Compound Interest Formula | Algebra 1 Notes & Key
A64.ican: use the compound interest formula and rewrite a growth expression for a different period.
A64.key_rule: A rate compounded n times a year pays r/n each period. To find an EQUAL rate for a different period, take a root or a power of the factor; never just divide or multiply the rate.
A64.key_rule_hint: Change the exponent to match the new period. Round only at the end.

watch.text: A student says 69% a year is the same as 34.5% each half year.
watch.right_why: 1.3² = 1.69: 30% each half year.

A64.learn: Students learn to use A = P(1 + r/n)ⁿᵗ, and rewrite a growth expression with a power or a root of its factor to show the rate for a different period.
A64.watchout: a wrong and a right rewrite of 69% yearly growth as a half-year rate side by side; the wrong one halves it to 34.5%, but 1.3² = 1.69, so it is 30%.
mistakes: Divides the yearly rate by the number of periods
Multiplies a period rate up to get the yearly rate
Compounds once a year instead of each quarter
Takes a root of the factor but keeps the exponent t

standards.text: Use the properties of exponents to transform expressions for exponential functions. For example the expression 1.15ᵗ can be rewritten as (1.15^(1/12))^(12t) ≈ 1.012^(12t) to reveal the approximate equivalent monthly interest rate if the annual rate is 15%.

A65.title: Linear and Exponential Functions Worksheet | Linear vs Exponential | Algebra 1
A65.ican: tell a linear table from an exponential one and say which function is larger in the long run.
A65.key_rule: A linear function adds the same step forever; with b > 1, an exponential's step keeps increasing, so it ends up ahead and stays ahead.
A65.key_rule_hint: Every exponential function compared on this sheet has a > 0 and b > 1.

watch.text: At t = 3, y = 50t gives 150 and y = 3ᵗ gives 27. A student says 50t stays ahead.
watch.wrong_why: One value of t cannot show the long run.
watch.right_why: Look further out: from t = 6 on, 3ᵗ is larger.

A65.learn: Students learn to test every difference and every ratio to tell linear from exponential, and compare the two further out, because a growing exponential ends up ahead.
A65.watchout: a wrong and a right comparison of y = 50t and y = 3ᵗ; the wrong one says 50t stays ahead since it leads at t = 3, but 3ᵗ wins by t = 6.
mistakes: Decides from one value of t that the leader stays ahead
Checks only the first difference
Checks only the first ratio
Calls a table linear because it adds more each time
Reads a power such as 6⁵ as 6 times 5

standards.text: Distinguish between situations that can be modeled with linear functions and with exponential functions.
Observe using graphs and tables that a quantity increasing exponentially eventually exceeds a quantity increasing linearly, quadratically, or (more generally) as a polynomial function.

A66.title: Writing Exponential Functions from Two Points & Tables Worksheet | Algebra 1
A66.ican: write y = a · bˣ from two points or a table by counting the steps between them.
A66.key_rule: Divide the later y by the earlier y, then take the root that matches the steps; points one step apart give b directly.
A66.key_rule_hint: Every b on this sheet is positive, so b² = 9 means b = 3.

watch.text: From (0, 5) and (2, 45), a student divides 45 ÷ 5 = 9 and writes y = 5 · 9ˣ.
watch.wrong_why: At x = 2 it gives 5 · 81 = 405, not 45.
watch.right_why: The points are 2 steps apart; 5 · 3² = 45.

A66.learn: Students learn to count the steps between two points, divide one output by the other to get b to that power, find b and a, and test the model on every point.
A66.watchout: a wrong and a right model through (0, 5) and (2, 45) side by side; the wrong one calls the ratio 9 the base, but the points are 2 steps apart, so b = 3.
mistakes: Calls the ratio of outputs b when the points are several steps apart
Takes the first y-value as a with no point at x = 0
Stops after testing only the two points used

standards.text: Construct linear and exponential functions, including arithmetic and geometric sequences, given a graph, a description of a relationship, or two input-output pairs (include reading these from a table).

A67.title: Classifying Polynomials by Degree & Number of Terms Worksheet | Algebra 1 Notes
A67.ican: write a polynomial in standard form and name its degree, leading coefficient and number of terms.
A67.key_rule: Combine like terms first, then read the degree from the highest term, wherever it sits.
A67.key_rule_hint: 1, 2 or 3 terms; four or more is just a polynomial. Not polynomials: 5x⁻¹ − 2 and 3/x.

watch.text: For 6x² + 2x⁵ − 1, a student gives the degree as 2.
watch.wrong_why: The first term is not always the highest.
watch.right_why: 2x⁵ has the highest exponent, wherever it sits.

A67.learn: Students learn to combine like terms, write a polynomial in standard form, and name its degree, its leading coefficient and its number of terms.
A67.watchout: a wrong and a right degree for 6x² + 2x⁵ − 1 side by side; the wrong one reads degree 2 off the first term, but 2x⁵ makes the degree 5.
mistakes: Reads the degree off the first term
Counts terms before combining like terms
Uses the larger exponent as the degree of a term with two variables
Adds the exponents when combining like terms
Drops the minus from the leading coefficient

standards.text: Understand that polynomials form a system analogous to the integers, namely, they are closed under the operations of addition, subtraction, and multiplication; add, subtract, and multiply polynomials.

A68.title: Adding and Subtracting Polynomials Worksheet | Polynomial Operations | Algebra 1
A68.ican: add and subtract polynomials, giving the minus sign to every term of the second one.
A68.key_rule: When subtracting, change the sign of each term in the second ( ), not just the first; then combine like terms and write the answer in standard form.
A68.key_rule_hint: If every term cancels, the answer is 0.

watch.text: For (6x² − 2x + 5) − (x² + 3x − 4), a student changes only the first sign.
watch.wrong_why: +3x and −4 kept their signs.
watch.right_why: All three signs change; the first term is right either way.

A68.learn: Students learn to add polynomials by combining like terms, and subtract them by changing the sign of every term in the second parentheses, then write the answer in standard form.
A68.watchout: a wrong and a right subtraction of (6x² − 2x + 5) − (x² + 3x − 4); the wrong one changes only the first sign and gets 5x² + x + 1.
mistakes: Applies the minus to the first term only
Treats subtracting a negative term as subtracting
Subtracts in the wrong order
Adds the exponents when adding like terms

standards.text: Understand that polynomials form a system analogous to the integers, namely, they are closed under the operations of addition, subtraction, and multiplication; add, subtract, and multiply polynomials.

A69.title: Multiplying Binomials Worksheet | FOIL Method | Monomials & Binomials Algebra 1
A69.ican: multiply a monomial or a binomial by a binomial, making every product.
A69.key_rule: Multiply every term of one factor by every term of the other, then combine like terms and write the answer in standard form.
A69.key_rule_hint: Count the products first: rows × columns.
A69.key_formula: (a + b)(c + d) = ac + ad + bc + bd

watch.text: For (x + 4)(x + 6), a student multiplies only the firsts and the lasts.
watch.wrong_why: x · 6 and 4 · x were never made.
watch.right_why: Four products; the middle two combine.

A69.learn: Students learn to multiply a monomial or a binomial by a binomial: they make every product, combine like terms and write the answer in standard form.
A69.watchout: a wrong and a right product of (x + 4)(x + 6) side by side; the wrong one multiplies only the firsts and the lasts, getting x² + 24.
mistakes: Multiplies only the first terms and the last terms
Drops the minus of a negative term in one of its products
Treats a negative times a negative as negative
Multiplies the exponents instead of adding them

standards.text: Understand that polynomials form a system analogous to the integers, namely, they are closed under the operations of addition, subtraction, and multiplication; add, subtract, and multiply polynomials.

A70.title: Multiplying Polynomials Worksheet | Multiplying Trinomials | Algebra 1 Notes
A70.ican: multiply polynomials, using every term of both factors.
A70.key_rule: Multiply each term of one factor by each term of the other, then combine like terms and write the answer in standard form.
A70.key_rule_hint: Check that every term of both factors was used.

watch.text: For (x + 4)(x² + 2x + 3), a student uses FOIL.
watch.wrong_why: 2x was never used: 2x² and 8x are missing.
watch.right_why: 6 products: every term of both factors.

A70.learn: Students learn to multiply polynomials: they multiply every term of one factor by every term of the other, combine like terms by degree and write the answer in standard form.
A70.watchout: a wrong and a right product of (x + 4)(x² + 2x + 3) side by side; the wrong one uses FOIL, so the 2x is never multiplied.
mistakes: Uses FOIL on a trinomial, so its middle term is never multiplied
Drops the minus of a negative term in one of its products
Treats a negative times a negative as negative
Stops before every like term is combined

standards.text: Understand that polynomials form a system analogous to the integers, namely, they are closed under the operations of addition, subtraction, and multiplication; add, subtract, and multiply polynomials.

A71.title: Special Products of Polynomials Worksheet | Squaring Binomials | Algebra 1 Notes
A71.ican: square a binomial and multiply a sum by a difference, keeping the middle term right.
A71.key_rule: In (a + b)² the equal outer and inner products double. In (a + b)(a − b) they are opposites and cancel.
A71.key_rule_hint: In a square, the middle term is ±2ab: 2 times the product of the two terms.

watch.text: For (x + 6)², a student squares each term.
watch.wrong_why: The outer and inner products are missing.
watch.right_why: (x + 6)(x + 6) has 4 products.

A71.learn: Students learn to square a binomial and multiply a sum by a difference: they double the equal outer and inner products, or cancel the opposite ones, and write the answer in standard form.
A71.watchout: a wrong and a right square of (x + 6)² side by side; the wrong one squares each term to get x² + 36 and misses the middle term 12x.
mistakes: Squares each term of a sum and misses the middle term
Gets the sign of the last term wrong
Does not square the coefficient of the variable
Uses only one of the two equal middle products

standards.text: Use the structure of an expression to identify ways to rewrite it. For example, see x⁴ - y⁴ as (x²)² - (y²)², thus recognizing it as a difference of squares that can be factored as (x² - y²)(x² + y²).

A72.skill: Factoring Out the Greatest Common Factor
A72.title: Factoring Out the GCF Worksheet | Greatest Common Factor | Algebra 1 Notes & Key
A72.ican: factor out the greatest common factor of a polynomial and check it by multiplying back.
A72.key_rule: Divide every term by the GCF; a term equal to the GCF leaves 1, not a blank. Multiply back to check.
A72.key_rule_hint: Then read the ( ): if its terms share a factor other than one, the GCF was not the greatest.

watch.text: For 7x² + 7x, a student writes 7x(x).
watch.wrong_why: 7x(x) multiplies back to only 7x².
watch.right_why: A term equal to the GCF leaves 1.

A72.learn: Students learn to find the GCF of a polynomial's terms, write the polynomial as the GCF times a parenthesized factor, and verify that it multiplies back and that nothing common is left.
A72.watchout: a wrong and a right factoring of 7x² + 7x side by side; the wrong one writes 7x(x), leaving a blank where the 1 belongs, instead of 7x(x + 1).
mistakes: Leaves a blank where a 1 belongs
Divides the exponents instead of subtracting them
Keeps the signs when dividing by a negative GCF
Takes out a common factor that is not the greatest

standards.text: Use the structure of an expression to identify ways to rewrite it. For example, see x⁴ - y⁴ as (x²)² - (y²)², thus recognizing it as a difference of squares that can be factored as (x² - y²)(x² + y²).

A73.title: Factoring Trinomials When a = 1 Worksheet | Factoring Quadratics | Algebra 1
A73.ican: factor x² + bx + c by finding the pair that multiplies to c and adds to b.
A73.key_rule: List the pairs that multiply to c. Use the one that adds to b, then check by multiplying back.
A73.key_rule_hint: Here p · q = c and p + q = b: the pair has two jobs.

watch.text: For x² + 2x − 15, a student writes (x − 5)(x + 3).
watch.wrong_why: It multiplies back to x² − 2x − 15.
watch.right_why: The pair must add to +2, not −2.

A73.learn: Students learn to factor a trinomial x² + bx + c into (x + p)(x + q) by finding the pair with product c and sum b, using the signs of b and c, and verify it by multiplying back.
A73.watchout: a wrong and a right factoring of x² + 2x − 15 side by side; the wrong one writes (x − 5)(x + 3), which multiplies back to x² − 2x − 15.
mistakes: Swaps the signs, so the product is right but the sum is wrong
Makes both numbers positive when b is negative
Stops at a pair that multiplies to c but does not add to b
Writes a factor's sign apart from its number

standards.text: Factor a quadratic expression to reveal the zeros of the function it defines.

A74.skill: Factoring Trinomials with a Leading Coefficient
A74.title: Factoring Trinomials When a Is Not 1 Worksheet | AC Method | Algebra 1 Notes
A74.ican: factor ax² + bx + c by finding the pair that multiplies to a · c and adds to b.
A74.key_rule: Multiply a · c, find the pair that adds to b, split the middle term, then read the box's edges.
A74.key_rule_hint: When a = 1, a · c is just c: the same two jobs as before.
A74.key_formula: p · q = a · c and p + q = b

watch.text: A student says 3x² + 7x + 2 does not factor: no pair of 2 adds to 7.
watch.wrong_why: The pair multiplies to a · c, not to c.
watch.right_why: It factors: the pair is 1 and 6.

A74.learn: Students learn to factor a trinomial ax² + bx + c: they take out any GCF, find the pair with product a · c and sum b, split the middle term, read the factors off the box and verify by multiplying back.
A74.watchout: a wrong and a right answer to whether 3x² + 7x + 2 factors; the wrong one looks for a pair from 2 alone, but a · c = 6 gives 1 and 6.
mistakes: Looks for the pair from c alone and says it does not factor
Swaps the constants between the two factors
Gets the signs in the factors wrong
Leaves out or skips the GCF

standards.text: Factor a quadratic expression to reveal the zeros of the function it defines.

A75.title: Factoring Difference of Squares Worksheet | Special Cases | Algebra 1 Notes
A75.ican: factor a difference of squares a² − b² as (a + b)(a − b) and tell when a sum of squares does not factor.
A75.key_rule: Root both squares and write one ( ) with + and one with −. Take out any GCF first.
A75.key_rule_hint: x² + 16 has no pair with product 16 and sum 0: same-sign numbers never add to 0.

watch.text: A student factors x² + 16 as (x + 4)(x − 4).
watch.wrong_why: That multiplies back to x² − 16.
watch.right: same-sign pairs of 16 never add to 0
watch.right_why: So x² + 16 does not factor over the integers.

A75.learn: Students learn to factor a difference of squares by rooting every part, take out a GCF first, factor completely, and explain why x² + c with c > 0 does not factor over the integers.
A75.watchout: a wrong and a right look at x² + 16 side by side; the wrong one factors it as (x + 4)(x − 4), which multiplies back to x² − 16.
mistakes: Factors a sum of squares as if it were a difference
Uses a number instead of its square root in the factors
Stops before the answer is factored completely
Uses the same sign in both factors

standards.text: Use the structure of an expression to identify ways to rewrite it. For example, see x⁴ - y⁴ as (x²)² - (y²)², thus recognizing it as a difference of squares that can be factored as (x² - y²)(x² + y²).

A76.title: Factoring Perfect Square Trinomials Worksheet | Special Cases | Algebra 1 Notes
A76.ican: test the middle term of a trinomial and factor a perfect square trinomial as a binomial squared.
A76.key_rule: Root both ends and double their product. Only a matching middle term gives (a ± b)²; check by multiplying back.
A76.key_rule_hint: x² + 6x + 4 is not one: 2 · x · 2 = 4x, not 6x.

watch.text: A student writes x² + 26x + 25 = (x + 5)².
watch.wrong_why: (x + 5)² has middle term 10x, not 26x.
watch.right_why: Square ends are not enough: test the middle.

A76.learn: Students learn to root the end terms, test whether the middle term is 2 times their product, factor a perfect square trinomial as (a + b)² or (a − b)², and factor a near miss with a pair instead.
A76.watchout: a wrong and a right factoring of x² + 26x + 25 side by side; the wrong one writes (x + 5)², whose middle term is 10x, instead of (x + 1)(x + 25).
mistakes: Checks the end terms but not the middle term
Loses or doubts the sign of the middle term
Mixes up a perfect square with a difference of squares
Leaves a GCF inside a factor

standards.text: Use the structure of an expression to identify ways to rewrite it. For example, see x⁴ - y⁴ as (x²)² - (y²)², thus recognizing it as a difference of squares that can be factored as (x² - y²)(x² + y²).

A77.title: Factoring Polynomials by Grouping Worksheet | Four Terms | Algebra 1 Notes & Key
A77.ican: factor a four-term polynomial by grouping, using the matching binomial as a check.
A77.key_rule: Both pairs must leave the same binomial. If they differ, recheck each GCF or reorder the terms.
A77.key_rule_hint: Every polynomial on this sheet starts with a positive term.
A77.key_formula: a(x + k) + b(x + k) = (x + k)(a + b)

watch.text: A student factors 2x³ + 6x² − 5x − 15 and writes 2x²(x + 3) − 5(x − 3).
watch.wrong_why: −5(x − 3) is −5x + 15, and the binomials differ.
watch.right_why: With −5 out, both pairs leave x + 3.

A77.learn: Students learn to split four terms into two pairs, take the GCF out of each (a negative one when the second pair starts with a minus), factor out the matching binomial, and test whether a factor factors again.
A77.watchout: a wrong and a right grouping of 2x³ + 6x² − 5x − 15 side by side; the wrong one writes −5(x − 3), so the binomials do not match, instead of −5(x + 3).
mistakes: Gets the sign wrong in the GCF or inside the parentheses
Gives up when the pairs in the given order share nothing
Stops before every factor is finished
Leaves the grouped sum as the answer

standards.text: Use the structure of an expression to identify ways to rewrite it. For example, see x⁴ - y⁴ as (x²)² - (y²)², thus recognizing it as a difference of squares that can be factored as (x² - y²)(x² + y²).

A78.title: Factoring Polynomials Completely Worksheet | Factoring Review | Algebra 1 Notes
A78.ican: choose a factoring method by taking out the GCF first and counting the terms left.
A78.key_rule: Take out the GCF first. Then the number of terms left picks the method; check each factor before you stop.
A78.key_rule_hint: On this sheet, a quadratic with no pattern and no pair does not factor.

watch.text: A student factors 4x² − 100 as (2x + 10)(2x − 10).
watch.wrong_why: It multiplies back, but 2x + 10 still shares 2.
watch.right_why: Take out the GCF first; then nothing is left to share.

A78.learn: Students learn to take out the GCF, count the terms left to choose the difference of squares, a trinomial method or grouping, factor completely, and tell when a quadratic does not factor.
A78.watchout: a wrong and a right factoring of 4x² − 100 side by side; the wrong one writes (2x + 10)(2x − 10), which still shares 2, instead of 4(x + 5)(x − 5).
mistakes: Uses a pattern before taking out the GCF
Factors a sum of squares as a difference
Writes a perfect square without testing the middle term
Stops when the GCF is 1
Stops before every factor is finished
Drops the GCF from the final answer

standards.text: Use the structure of an expression to identify ways to rewrite it. For example, see x⁴ - y⁴ as (x²)² - (y²)², thus recognizing it as a difference of squares that can be factored as (x² - y²)(x² + y²).

A79.title: Graphing Quadratics Worksheet | Vertex, Axis of Symmetry & Parabolas | Algebra 1
A79.ican: graph y = ax² + bx + c by finding the axis of symmetry and the vertex first.
A79.key_rule: Find the axis x = −b/(2a) first; the vertex is on it. Points the same distance from the axis have the same height.
A79.key_rule_hint: The sign of a, not c, says which way the parabola opens.
A79.key_formula: y = ax² + bx + c; axis x = −b/(2a)

watch.text: A student says the axis of symmetry of y = x² − 6x + 5 is x = −3.
watch.wrong_why: b is −6, so −b is +6: the minus was dropped.
watch.right_why: x = 2 and x = 4 both give −3, and 3 is halfway.

A79.learn: Students learn to find the axis of symmetry x = −b/(2a) and the vertex, give the y-intercept and the direction, and use symmetry to plot points and graph a parabola.
A79.watchout: a wrong and a right axis of symmetry for y = x² − 6x + 5; the wrong one drops the minus in −b and gets x = −3 instead of x = 3.
mistakes: Drops the minus in x = −b/(2a)
Reads the direction of opening from c instead of a
Mirrors points across the y-axis instead of the axis of symmetry
Divides by a instead of 2a
Squares a negative input without parentheses

standards.text: Graph linear and quadratic functions and show intercepts, maxima, and minima.

A80.title: Key Features of Quadratic Functions Worksheet | Parabolas | Algebra 1 Notes
A80.ican: name a parabola's vertex, axis of symmetry, intercepts, domain, range and intervals.
A80.key_rule: The domain of y = ax² + bx + c is all real numbers (unless a context limits it). The range starts at the vertex's y and runs one way: y ≥ k when it opens upward, y ≤ k when it opens downward.
A80.key_rule_hint: Increasing and decreasing use <; the range uses ≥ or ≤, because k itself is an output.

watch.text: A student says y = x² − 8x + 10 has domain and range all real numbers.
watch.wrong_why: It turns at (4, −6): no output is below −6.
watch.right: domain: all real numbers; range: y ≥ −6
watch.right_why: The domain half was right; the range starts at the vertex.

A80.learn: Students learn to give the vertex and its maximum or minimum value, the axis of symmetry as an equation, the intercepts as points, the domain and range, and where a parabola increases and decreases.
A80.watchout: a wrong and a right domain and range for y = x² − 8x + 10 side by side; the wrong one gives the range as all real numbers, but it is y ≥ −6.
mistakes: Gives the range of a parabola as all real numbers
Gives where the minimum or maximum occurs as its value
Runs the range the wrong way from the vertex
Writes the axis of symmetry as a number instead of an equation
Reads an interval past the vertex or from right to left

standards.text: For a function that models a relationship between two quantities, interpret key features of graphs and tables in terms of the quantities, and sketch graphs showing key features given a verbal description of the relationship. Key features include: intercepts; intervals where the function is increasing, decreasing, positive, or negative; relative maximums and minimums; symmetries; end behavior; and periodicity.

A81.title: Vertex Form Worksheet | Transformations of Quadratic Functions | Algebra 1 Notes
A81.ican: read the vertex from vertex form and describe the graph as moves of y = x².
A81.key_rule: In y = a(x − h)² + k the vertex is (h, k). A number inside the bracket moves the graph the opposite way to its sign; k moves it as written.
A81.key_rule_hint: To check a vertex, put x = h in: the bracket is 0, so y comes out as k.

watch.text: A student says y = (x + 4)² − 2 has vertex (4, −2).
watch.wrong_why: The form subtracts h: x + 4 is x − (−4).
watch.right_why: At x = −4 the bracket is 0 and y = −2.

A81.learn: Students learn to read the vertex (h, k) from y = a(x − h)² + k with the sign of h right, verify it by putting x = h in, and describe the graph as a flip, stretch and moves of y = x².
A81.watchout: a wrong and a right vertex for y = (x + 4)² − 2 side by side; the wrong one reads h as 4, giving (4, −2), instead of (−4, −2).
mistakes: Reads the sign of h as printed instead of reversing it
Reverses the sign of k as well as h
Leaves out the stretch or flip that a causes
Lets a negative a change the vertex

standards.text: Identify the effect on the graph of replacing f(x) by f(x) + k, k f(x), f(kx), and f(x + k) for specific values of k (both positive and negative); find the value of k given the graphs. Experiment with cases and illustrate an explanation of the effects on the graph using technology. Include recognizing even and odd functions from their graphs and algebraic expressions for them.

A82.skill: Completing the Square to Find the Vertex
A82.title: Standard Form to Vertex Form Worksheet | Completing the Square | Algebra 1 Notes
A82.ican: complete the square to write a quadratic in vertex form and read the vertex.
A82.key_rule: For y = x² + bx + c (factor a out first when a ≠ 1), add (b/2)² and subtract it on the same side, so the rule does not change. Then read the vertex.
A82.key_rule_hint: With a in front, the number is added inside a( ), so a times the number you added comes back out.

watch.text: A student writes y = x² + 6x + 2 as y = (x + 3)² + 2.
watch.wrong_why: Adding 9 changed the rule: this is x² + 6x + 11.
watch.right_why: Add 9 and subtract 9: the rule stays the same.

A82.learn: Students learn to add and subtract (b/2)² on the same side to rewrite y = x² + bx + c in vertex form (factoring a out first when a ≠ 1), verify by expanding, and read the vertex.
A82.watchout: a wrong and a right vertex form of y = x² + 6x + 2; the wrong one adds 9 but never subtracts it, so it writes (x + 3)² + 2.
mistakes: Adds (b/2)² and never subtracts it
Loses the sign of half of b
Halves b but does not square it
Subtracts the number added inside the parentheses instead of a times it
Combines the constants with the wrong sign

standards.text: Use the process of factoring and completing the square in a quadratic function to show zeros, extreme values, and symmetry of the graph, and interpret these in terms of a context.

A83.title: Factored Form of a Quadratic Worksheet | Zeros & Roots of Quadratics | Algebra 1
A83.ican: read the zeros from factored form and use them to find the axis and the vertex.
A83.key_rule: The zeros of y = a(x − p)(x − q) are p and q: x + 8 is 0 at x = −8, not 8. The number a in front does not move the zeros.
A83.key_rule_hint: Check a zero: put it in, and one bracket must give 0.

watch.text: A student says y = (x + 3)(x − 6) has zeros 3 and −6.
watch.wrong_why: Those are the numbers printed, signs and all.

A83.learn: Students learn to read the zeros p and q from y = a(x − p)(x − q) with the right signs, find the axis halfway between them, the vertex and the y-intercept, and expand to standard form.
A83.watchout: a wrong and a right pair of zeros for y = (x + 3)(x − 6) side by side; the wrong one reads the printed numbers, 3 and −6, instead of −3 and 6.
mistakes: Reads the zeros as the numbers printed in the factors
Uses half the distance between the zeros as the axis
Leaves out the leading coefficient when finding a y-value
Gives the vertex a y-value of 0, as if it were a zero
Misses the zero from a lone x factor

standards.text: Identify zeros of polynomials when suitable factorizations are available, and use the zeros to construct a rough graph of the function defined by the polynomial.

A84.skill: Average Rate of Change for Quadratics
A84.title: Average Rate of Change Worksheet | Quadratic Functions | Algebra 1 Notes & Key
A84.ican: find a quadratic's average rate of change over an interval and say why the interval matters.
A84.key_rule: For a quadratic, the average rate of change depends on the interval; for a line it is the same on every interval.
A84.key_rule_hint: In a context, give units: output units per input unit, such as feet per second.

watch.text: A student says f(x) = x² − 3 has average rate of change 4.
watch.wrong_why: A quadratic has no one rate: it depends on the interval.
watch.right_why: Name the interval: the rate changes with it.

A84.learn: Students learn to find the average rate of change (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a) over a stated interval, with units in a context, and explain why a quadratic's rate depends on the interval.
A84.watchout: a wrong and a right average rate of change for f(x) = x² − 3; the wrong one gives one rate, 4, but it is 4 on [1, 3] and 8 on [3, 5].
mistakes: Gives a quadratic one rate of change with no interval
Forgets to divide by the change in x
Loses the sign of a negative function value
Drops the sign when substituting a negative x into −x
Subtracts in opposite orders on the top and bottom
Divides by the end x-value instead of the run

standards.text: Calculate and interpret the average rate of change of a function (presented symbolically or as a table) over a specified interval. Estimate the rate of change from a graph.

A85.title: Modeling with Quadratic Functions | First and Second Differences | Algebra 1
A85.ican: use second differences to tell when data is quadratic and to build its model.
A85.key_rule: Not linear does not mean no pattern: take the second differences. If they are all the same (not 0), a quadratic fits.
A85.key_rule_hint: Table from x = 0 in steps of 1: c is the y at 0, and b = (y at 1 − y at 0) − a.

watch.text: At x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 the y-values are 2, 4, 8, 14, 22. A student says the differences 2, 4, 6, 8 are not all the same, so there is no pattern.
watch.wrong_why: Not linear is not the same as no pattern.
watch.right_why: Take the next row: the jumps grow by 2 each time.

A85.learn: Students learn to take first and second differences of a table with equal x-steps, decide whether it is linear or quadratic, write y = ax² + bx + c from the differences, and use the model in a context.
A85.watchout: a wrong and a right reading of y-values 2, 4, 8, 14, 22 side by side; the wrong one says no pattern, but the second differences are all 2, so a quadratic fits.
mistakes: Stops when the first differences change and says there is no pattern
Takes a as the whole second difference instead of half of it
Calls a table with second differences of 0 quadratic
Uses the first difference as b
Subtracts each y-value from the one before it
Reads c as the first y when the table starts after x = 0

standards.text: Determine an explicit expression, a recursive process, or steps for calculation from a context.

A86.title: Solving Quadratics by Graphing Worksheet | Zeros of a Quadratic | Algebra 1
A86.ican: solve a quadratic equation from its graph and say how many real solutions it has.
A86.key_rule: Read the solutions where the parabola crosses or touches the x-axis. It turns, so after one crossing, look for a second.
A86.key_rule_hint: Opens up: vertex below the x-axis, two; on it, one; above it, none.

watch.text: A student solves x² − 6x + 8 = 0 by graphing, finds x = 4 and stops.
watch.wrong_why: One crossing; the parabola turns and crosses again.

A86.learn: Students learn to solve ax² + bx + c = 0 by reading where the graph of y = ax² + bx + c meets the x-axis, find every solution (two, one or none), and verify each one in the equation.
A86.watchout: a wrong and a right graphical solution of x² − 6x + 8 = 0 side by side; the wrong one finds x = 4 and stops, missing the second crossing at x = 2.
mistakes: Finds one crossing and stops
Drops the negative sign of a crossing left of the y-axis
Reads the y-intercept as a solution
Gives the y-values of the crossings instead of the x-values
Says a vertex above the x-axis means no solution, even opening down
Gives the vertex, or two solutions, when the parabola only touches the axis

standards.text: Explain why the x-coordinates of the points where the graphs of the equations y = f(x) and y = g(x) intersect are the solutions of the equation f(x) = g(x); find the solutions approximately, e.g., using technology to graph the functions, make tables of values, or find successive approximations. Include cases where f(x) and/or g(x) are linear, polynomial, rational, absolute value, exponential, and logarithmic functions.

A87.skill: Solving by Factoring and the Zero Product Property
A87.title: Solving Quadratics by Factoring | Zero Product Property Worksheet | Algebra 1
A87.ican: solve a quadratic equation by getting 0 on one side, factoring and setting each factor to 0.
A87.key_rule: Get 0 alone on one side first. Then set each factor with x equal to 0 and solve each one.
A87.key_rule_hint: Write the solutions together with 'or', then check each in the original.

watch.text: To solve (x − 3)(x + 1) = 12, a student writes x − 3 = 12 or x + 1 = 12.
watch.wrong_why: 12 is not 0: a product of 12 says nothing about either factor.

A87.learn: Students learn to solve a quadratic equation by factoring: they move every term to one side so the other is 0, factor fully, set each factor equal to 0, and verify each solution in the original equation.
A87.watchout: a wrong and a right solution of (x − 3)(x + 1) = 12 side by side; the wrong one sets each factor equal to 12 instead of first making one side 0.
mistakes: Sets each factor equal to a number that is not 0
Reads the solutions' signs straight off the factors
Counts a constant factor as giving a solution
Drops the constant when moving every term to one side
Factors with the signs swapped
Divides both sides by x and loses the solution x = 0

standards.text: Solve quadratic equations by inspection (e.g., for x² = 49), taking square roots, completing the square, the quadratic formula and factoring, as appropriate to the initial form of the equation. Recognize when the quadratic formula gives complex solutions and write them as a ± bi for real numbers a and b.

A88.title: Solving Quadratics by Square Roots Worksheet | Square Root Method | Algebra 1
A88.ican: solve x² = k and (x − h)² = k by taking both square roots.
A88.key_rule: Get x² by itself first. If k > 0, x² = k gives x = ±√k: two solutions. k = 0 gives one; k < 0 gives none.
A88.key_rule_hint: (x − h)² = k with k ≥ 0: x − h = ±√k, so x = h ± √k.

watch.text: A student solves x² = 49 and writes x = 7.
watch.wrong_why: That is only the positive root.
watch.right_why: (−7)² = 49 too: squaring hides the sign.

A88.learn: Students learn to solve x² = k and (x − h)² = k: they get the square alone, take both square roots, finish solving for x, give exact answers in simplest radical form, and say when there is no real solution.
A88.watchout: a wrong and a right solution of x² = 49 side by side; the wrong one gives only x = 7, but (−7)² = 49 too, so x = 7 or x = −7.
mistakes: Takes only the positive square root
Halves the number instead of taking its square root
Undoes an added constant by adding
Stops before solving for x after taking the root
Gives real answers when the square equals a negative number
Multiplies instead of dividing to get x² alone

standards.text: Solve quadratic equations by inspection (e.g., for x² = 49), taking square roots, completing the square, the quadratic formula and factoring, as appropriate to the initial form of the equation. Recognize when the quadratic formula gives complex solutions and write them as a ± bi for real numbers a and b.

A89.skill: Solving Quadratics by Completing the Square
A89.title: Solving Quadratics by Completing the Square Worksheet | Algebra 1 Notes & Key
A89.ican: solve a quadratic equation by completing the square on both sides.
A89.key_rule: With x² + bx = c, add (b/2)² to both sides. The left side becomes (x + b/2)², a perfect square.
A89.key_rule_hint: Then take ± roots (if the right side is ≥ 0) and find x; a negative right side means no real solution. If a ≠ 1, divide every term by a first.

watch.text: A student adds 4 to only the left side of x² − 4x = 5.
watch.wrong_why: The 4 went on the left only.

A89.learn: Students learn to solve a quadratic equation by completing the square: they get x² + bx = c, add (b/2)² to both sides, take square roots (keeping ±), and give exact answers in simplest radical form.
A89.watchout: a wrong and a right start to solving x² − 4x = 5 by completing the square; the wrong one adds 4 to the left side only.
mistakes: Adds (b/2)² to the left side only
Adds half of b without squaring it
Loses the sign of half of a negative b
Subtracts the wrong way when finishing the solution
Divides only the x terms by the leading coefficient
Leaves a radical unsimplified, or keeps a negative length in a story

standards.text: Use the method of completing the square to transform any quadratic equation in x into an equation of the form (x - p)² = q that has the same solutions. Derive the quadratic formula from this form.

A90.title: Quadratic Formula Worksheet | Solving Quadratic Equations | Algebra 1 Notes
A90.ican: solve a quadratic equation with the quadratic formula.
A90.key_rule: Get ax² + bx + c = 0 first. Then x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/(2a), with the whole top over 2a.
A90.key_rule_hint: a ≠ 0. Real solutions need b² − 4ac ≥ 0; on this sheet it is always positive.

watch.text: A student solving 2x² − 7x − 4 = 0 writes x = 7 ± 9/4.
watch.wrong_why: Only the root was divided by 4.
watch.right_why: (7 ± 9)/4: the bar divides the 7 too.

A90.learn: Students learn to solve ax² + bx + c = 0 with the quadratic formula: they write it = 0 first, read a, b and c with their signs, divide the whole top by 2a, and simplify fully.
A90.watchout: a wrong and a right finish to the quadratic formula for 2x² − 7x − 4 = 0 side by side; the wrong one divides only the root by 4, instead of (7 ± 9)/4.
mistakes: Divides only the square root part by 2a
Squares a negative b to a negative number
Drops the minus sign of c in −4ac
Divides by 2 instead of 2a
Reads a, b and c before the equation equals 0
Rounds before the final step

standards.text: Solve quadratic equations by inspection (e.g., for x² = 49), taking square roots, completing the square, the quadratic formula and factoring, as appropriate to the initial form of the equation. Recognize when the quadratic formula gives complex solutions and write them as a ± bi for real numbers a and b.

A91.skill: The Discriminant and Number of Solutions
A91.title: The Discriminant and Number of Solutions of a Quadratic | Algebra 1 Worksheet
A91.ican: use the discriminant to say how many real solutions a quadratic equation has.
A91.key_rule: For ax² + bx + c = 0, D = b² − 4ac. D > 0: two real solutions; D = 0: one; D < 0: no real solution.
A91.key_rule_hint: a ≠ 0. Write the equation = 0 first. Only the sign of D matters, not its size.

watch.text: A student finds D = 0 for x² − 6x + 9 = 0 and writes no real solution.
watch.wrong_why: Zero was read as nothing.

A91.learn: Students learn to write ax² + bx + c = 0, work out D = b² − 4ac, and say from its sign whether the equation has two, one or no real solutions, without solving it.
A91.watchout: a wrong and a right reading of D = 0 for x² − 6x + 9 = 0 side by side; the wrong one says no real solution, but there is one, x = 3.
mistakes: Reads a discriminant of 0 as no solution
Flips the sign of −4ac
Works out 4ac − b² instead of b² − 4ac
Leaves a out of 4ac
Reads does not factor as no real solution
Reads c before the equation equals 0, or squares a negative b as negative

standards.text: Solve quadratic equations by inspection (e.g., for x² = 49), taking square roots, completing the square, the quadratic formula and factoring, as appropriate to the initial form of the equation. Recognize when the quadratic formula gives complex solutions and write them as a ± bi for real numbers a and b.

A92.title: Linear-Quadratic Systems Worksheet | Nonlinear Systems of Equations | Algebra 1
A92.ican: solve a system of a line and a parabola and give every solution as a point.
A92.key_rule: Set the right sides equal and solve the quadratic: two, one or no solutions. Give each x its own y.
A92.key_rule_hint: Write the quadratic = 0 to solve it. Answer with points, and check every point in both equations.

watch.text: A student solves y = x² and y = x + 6 and answers (3, 9).
watch.wrong_why: One point; x = −2 was dropped.

A92.learn: Students learn to solve a system of a line and a parabola: they set the two rules for y equal, solve the quadratic, give each x its own y, and say whether there are two, one or no solutions.
A92.watchout: a wrong and a right solution of y = x² and y = x + 6 side by side; the wrong one gives only (3, 9) and drops the second point, (−2, 4).
mistakes: Stops at one intersection point
Gives only the x-values
Writes the y-coordinate first
Reads a discriminant of 0 as no solution
Moves a constant across the equal sign without changing its sign
Gives both x-values the same y-value

standards.text: Solve a simple system consisting of a linear equation and a quadratic equation in two variables algebraically and graphically. For example, find the points of intersection between the line y = -3x and the circle x² + y² = 3.

A93.skill: Dot Plots, Histograms, and Box Plots
A93.title: Histograms, Dot Plots, Box and Whisker Plots | Box Plots Worksheet | Algebra 1
A93.ican: read a dot plot, a histogram and a box plot, and count the values in each part.
A93.key_rule: Each of the four parts of a box plot holds about a quarter of the values. A wide part means its values are spread out, not that there are more of them.
A93.key_rule_hint: On this sheet, a histogram bar from 60 to 70 counts 60 ≤ x < 70: its left edge is in, its right edge out.
A93.key_formula: min · Q1 · median · Q3 · max: four parts

watch.text: A box plot of 16 scores has its box from 20 to 30 and its right whisker from 30 to 62. Lia says most of the scores are above 30.
watch.wrong: most of the 16 scores are above 30
watch.wrong_why: A long whisker is not a crowd.
watch.right_why: Each part holds about a quarter: 16 ÷ 4 = 4.

A93.learn: Students learn to read the same data as a dot plot, a histogram and a box plot, find the five-number summary, and count the values in each part of a box plot.
A93.watchout: a wrong and a right reading of a box plot of 16 scores with a long right whisker side by side; the wrong one says most scores are above 30, but only about 4 are.
mistakes: Reads a long part of a box plot as most of the data
Takes the middle of the number line as the median
Counts a histogram bar's right edge as part of that bar
Keeps the median in both halves when finding the quartiles
Counts only one whisker's quarter of the data
Finds the median before sorting the data

standards.text: Represent data with plots on the real number line (dot plots, histograms, and box plots).

A94.title: Standard Deviation & Interquartile Range | Measures of Center & Spread Algebra 1
A94.ican: find the mean, median, IQR and standard deviation, and say which pair describes the data.
A94.key_rule: The mean adds every value, so one value far from the rest pulls it toward that value. The median depends only on the middle of the ordered list.
A94.key_rule_hint: Pair the median with the IQR, and the mean with the SD. With no far values and a balanced shape, the mean and SD usually fit best.

watch.text: Eight salaries, in thousands of dollars: 22, 24, 25, 27, 28, 30, 33, 211. A student calls the mean, 50, the typical salary.
watch.wrong_why: Seven of the eight earn less than 50.
watch.right_why: 211 pulls the mean; the median sits among the salaries.

A94.learn: Students learn to find the mean, the median, the IQR and the standard deviation, see how one value far from the rest moves the mean but not the median, and pair each center with its spread.
A94.watchout: a wrong and a right typical salary for eight salaries, one of them far above the rest, side by side; the wrong one picks the mean, 50, instead of the median, 27.5.
mistakes: Calls the mean typical when one value is far from the rest
Takes the median of an unsorted list
Gives the range as the IQR
Stops before taking the square root for the standard deviation
Pairs the median with the range instead of the IQR
Averages the deviations without squaring them

standards.text: Use statistics appropriate to the shape of the data distribution to compare center (median, mean) and spread (interquartile range, standard deviation) of two or more different data sets.

A95.title: Identifying Outliers Worksheet | Comparing Distributions | Algebra 1 Notes & Key
A95.ican: test for outliers with the 1.5 × IQR rule and compare two data sets by center and spread.
A95.key_rule: A value is an outlier when it is more than 1.5 × IQR below Q1 or above Q3. It is unusual, not automatically wrong.
A95.key_rule_hint: With an outlier or a skewed shape, the median and IQR usually compare better; for symmetric data, the mean and standard deviation.
A95.key_formula: fences: Q1 − 1.5 × IQR and Q3 + 1.5 × IQR

watch.text: Rainfall on 9 days, in mm: 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 48. A real storm gave the 48, an outlier. A student deletes it as a mistake.
watch.wrong: delete 48: it must be a mistake
watch.wrong_why: Unusual is not the same as wrong.
watch.right_why: It is real data, and the median barely feels it.

A95.learn: Students learn to find the fences Q1 − 1.5 × IQR and Q3 + 1.5 × IQR, decide which values are outliers, see what an outlier does to the mean and the median, and compare two data sets with a fitting center and spread.
A95.watchout: a wrong and a right way to handle a real 48 mm storm day among 9 days of small rainfall totals; the wrong one deletes the outlier as a mistake instead of keeping it.
mistakes: Deletes a real outlier as a mistake
Leaves the 1.5 out of the fence formula
Compares means when one data set has an outlier
Reverses which way a long tail pulls the mean
Calls a value an outlier because it is far from its neighbor
Judges spread by the median and range alone

standards.text: Interpret differences in shape, center, and spread in the context of the data sets, accounting for possible effects of extreme data points (outliers).

A96.title: Two-Way Frequency Tables Worksheet | Conditional Relative Frequency | Algebra 1
A96.ican: find joint, marginal and conditional relative frequencies from a two-way table.
A96.key_rule: The words after "of the" name the group. Its total is the denominator.
A96.key_rule_hint: Round only at the end, to the place the question names.

watch.text: Of 100 students, 60 play a sport, and 18 of those 60 have a job. A student says 18% of the athletes have a job.
watch.wrong_why: 100 is everyone, not the athletes.
watch.right_why: The group is the 60 athletes.

A96.learn: Students learn to read a two-way table, find joint, marginal and conditional relative frequencies with the right denominator, and judge association by comparing row percents.
A96.watchout: a wrong and a right percent of athletes with a job when 18 of 60 athletes, out of 100 students, have one; the wrong one divides by 100 instead of 60.
mistakes: Divides by the grand total when the question names a group
Divides a joint frequency by a row total
Uses a column total for a row group
Uses a row total for a column group
Compares raw counts instead of percents to judge association
Treats the two conditional percents of one cell as equal

standards.text: Summarize categorical data for two categories in two-way frequency tables. Interpret relative frequencies in the context of the data (including joint, marginal, and conditional relative frequencies). Recognize possible associations and trends in the data.

A97.skill: Scatter Plots and Lines of Best Fit
A97.title: Scatter Plot & Line of Best Fit Worksheet | Trend Lines | Algebra 1 Notes & Key
A97.ican: judge a line of best fit, write its equation from two points on it, and predict with it.
A97.key_rule: About as many dots lie above a line of best fit as below it, and it follows the trend. How many it touches is not the test.
A97.key_rule_hint: Use two points ON the drawn line, where it crosses grid corners, not two data dots.
A97.key_formula: slope = rise ÷ run, on the line

watch.text: For the 8 dots in the graph above, a student picks y = x + 2 as the line of best fit because it passes through 3 of them.
watch.wrong: 3 dots on the line, so it fits best
watch.wrong_why: Touching dots is not the test.
watch.right_why: Not balanced, so not a line of best fit.

A97.learn: Students learn to describe the association in a scatter plot, judge a line of best fit by balance, write its equation from two points on the line, and predict inside the data.
A97.watchout: a wrong and a right judgment of a line through 3 of 8 dots; the wrong one calls it the line of best fit, but 1 other dot is above it and 4 below.
mistakes: Picks the line that touches the most dots
Uses run over rise for the slope
Loses the sign of a negative slope
Calls a prediction outside the data interpolation
Draws the line through the two end points
Reads b as a point's y-value when x is not 0

standards.text: Fit a function to the data; use functions fitted to data to solve problems in the context of the data. Use given functions or choose a function suggested by the context. Emphasize linear, quadratic, and exponential models.

A98.title: Residuals and Residual Plots Worksheet | Goodness of Fit | Algebra 1 Notes & Key
A98.ican: find residuals and read a residual plot to judge whether a line fits.
A98.key_rule: Random scatter around 0 suggests a good linear fit. A clear pattern means a line is not the right model.
A98.key_rule_hint: Judge the shape of the residual plot, not the sum of the residuals.

watch.text: For 8 points, a line of best fit gives residuals 7, 1, −3, −5, −5, −3, 1, 7. A student says a line is a good model because they add to 0.
watch.wrong_why: Adding to 0 says balanced, not straight.
watch.right_why: A pattern: the data curve, so not a line.

A98.learn: Students learn to find each residual as actual minus predicted, plot the residuals, and read the plot: random scatter suggests a good linear fit, a pattern does not.
A98.watchout: a wrong and a right reading of residuals 7, 1, −3, −5, −5, −3, 1, 7; the wrong one calls the fit good because they add to 0, but they form a U.
mistakes: Judges the fit by the sum of the residuals
Subtracts predicted minus actual
Decides above or below by the size of y instead of the prediction
Calls a residual plot a good fit when its dots form a pattern
Drops a residual's sign when finding the actual value
Thinks a residual plot with no pattern means exact predictions

standards.text: Informally assess the fit of a function by plotting and analyzing residuals.

A99.title: Correlation Coefficient & Causation | Correlation vs Causation | Algebra 1 Notes
A99.ican: describe a correlation coefficient and explain why correlation does not show causation.
A99.key_rule: Correlation is not causation: a lurking variable may drive both. A randomized experiment can show cause.
A99.key_rule_hint: On this sheet, ignore the sign: 0.8 or more is strong, 0.5 up to 0.8 is moderate, under 0.5 is weak.

watch.text: In a town, ice cream sales and drownings have r = 0.92. A student says ice cream causes drownings.
watch.wrong: r = 0.92 is high, so ice cream causes drownings
watch.wrong_why: A correlation alone cannot show cause.
watch.right: hot weather drives both: more ice cream, more swimming
watch.right_why: A lurking variable moves them together.

A99.learn: Students learn to read a correlation coefficient r for direction and strength, say what it does not measure, and explain why a correlation does not show that one variable causes another.
A99.watchout: a wrong and a right reading of r = 0.92 for ice cream sales and drownings side by side; the wrong one says ice cream causes drownings, but hot weather drives both.
mistakes: Reads a strong correlation as proof of cause
Compares signed r values instead of their sizes for strength
Reads r = 0 as no relationship instead of no linear association
Names one of the two variables as the lurking variable
Treats a self-chosen group as proof of cause
Reads a negative correlation as weak

standards.text: Compute (using technology) and interpret the correlation coefficient of a linear fit.
Distinguish between correlation and causation.
